title: What philosophy is
description: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about reality, knowledge and value, and answers them mainly by building and examining arguments.

facts.text: Philosophy asks deep, fundamental questions about the nature of the universe and ourselves, the limits of human knowledge and values, such as whether a law is fair; a physicist asks what caused an event, a philosopher whether causation exists at all.

Philosophical questions can’t be settled by purely empirical means: no lab experiment can test whether a society should value equality over freedom, though philosophers often use scientific findings as premises.
The main method of philosophy is to build and examine arguments: reasons, called premises, offered to support a conclusion.
When a question becomes open to rigorous experiment it tends to leave philosophy for its own field: the natural sciences were once called natural philosophy.
Most doctoral degrees are called Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), even in subjects such as chemistry.
Thales in Greece (about 620-546 BCE), Confucius in China (traditionally 551-479 BCE) and the Buddha in India (flourished about 450 BCE) lived within a few centuries of one another.

title: The branches of philosophy
description: Philosophy’s main branches each ask one kind of question: metaphysics (what exists), epistemology (what we can know), ethics (how to act and live), logic (good reasoning), aesthetics (beauty and art) and political philosophy (society and justice).

facts.text: Metaphysics studies what sorts of things exist, what the world is made of, and how things cause or explain each other.
Epistemology, from the Greek episteme (knowledge), studies knowledge, evidence and justified belief, such as whether we can trust our senses.
Ethics, or moral philosophy, asks what makes actions right or wrong and what makes a person or a life good.
Logic studies good and bad arguments and reasoning.
Aesthetics is the theory of beauty and, more broadly, the philosophy of art.
Political philosophy begins with the question of what a person’s relationship to society ought to be, and asks what makes a society just or unjust.

The word metaphysics comes from Ta meta ta phusika, ’the ones after the physical ones’, a title an editor, probably Andronicus of Rhodes, gave Aristotle’s books at least a century after his death; Aristotle never knew the word.

title: Thought experiments
description: A thought experiment tests an idea by imagining a carefully built case instead of running a real one, as in Galileo’s tied balls or Glaucon’s ring of Gyges; critics such as Kathleen Wilkes doubt how much they prove.

facts.text: Thought experiments are devices of the imagination: instead of running a real experiment, you imagine a scenario and reason about it; they are used in philosophy, physics, mathematics, economics and other fields.

Galileo imagined tying a heavy ball to a light one: on Aristotle’s view that heavier bodies fall faster, the pair would fall both slower (the light one holds back the heavy) and faster (together they are heavier), a contradiction.
In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of the shepherd Gyges, who finds a ring that makes him invisible and uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the kingdom.
Glaucon imagines giving one ring to a just person and one to an unjust person, and argues both would act alike, because people are just only when they cannot safely be unjust.
Kathleen Wilkes argued in Real People (1988) that thought experiments, especially about personal identity, give inconclusive and unconvincing results, and preferred real cases.

title: Plato’s Forms
description: Plato held that perfect, eternal, unchanging Forms such as Beauty, Equality or Circle, known by thought rather than the senses, are more real than the changing things we see; his own Parmenides raises the Third Man objection.

facts.text: Plato held that beyond the world our senses show us is a more real and perfect realm of Forms, such as Beauty, Justice and Equality, which are eternal and changeless.
Plato’s most basic distinction is between the many things that appear beautiful and the one Form that is what beauty really is; things are beautiful by sharing in, or participating in, that Form.
On a standard reading of Plato, the Form Circle is perfectly circular, while every drawn circle or round ball falls short of it.
For Plato the Forms are grasped by thought, not by the senses: they exist in a realm available only to thought.

In Plato’s Phaedo, Socrates argues that equal sticks and stones sometimes appear equal and sometimes unequal, while Equality itself never appears unequal, so our knowledge of Equality cannot have come from the sticks.

In Plato’s dialogue Parmenides, the Third Man argument (named by Aristotle) objects that if large things share the Form Large and that Form is itself large, a further Form is needed, and so on forever; scholars disagree whether Plato thought it fatal.

title: Aristotle’s four causes
description: Aristotle explained anything, such as a bronze statue, by four causes: material (what it is made of), formal (what it is), efficient (where the change came from) and final (what it is for); he placed form inside things, and Bacon later wanted final causes out of physics.

facts.text: Aristotle held that we know a thing only when we grasp its cause, its ’why’; his four causes are four kinds of answer to a why-question, and a full explanation can call on all four.
The material cause answers ’What is it made out of?’: for a bronze statue, the bronze.
The formal cause answers ’What is it?’: its form or essence; for a bronze statue, the shape the melted bronze is poured into.
The efficient cause answers ’Where does the change come from?’: for a bronze statue, Aristotle points most precisely to the art of bronze-casting in the sculptor.
The final cause is that for the sake of which something is done: the model, the mold and the melting and pouring of bronze are all for the sake of the finished statue.
Aristotle, who studied at Plato’s Academy, rejected Plato’s separately existing Forms: for him form exists in the thing, so a bronze sphere’s bronze and roundness are not two separate things.

In The Advancement of Learning (1605), Francis Bacon argued that final causes, such as clouds being ’for’ watering the earth, belong to metaphysics, and that mixing them into physics had held back the search for physical causes.

title: Confucius and the junzi
description: Confucius turned the junzi from a person of noble birth into a person of moral nobility, marked by ren (humaneness) expressed through li (ritual propriety) performed with real feeling; the Mohists attacked costly Confucian rituals.

facts.text: Confucius (traditionally 551-479 BCE) is known mainly through the Analects, an early text of his sayings and conversations with disciples.
The word junzi originally meant ’prince’s son’; Confucius was a pivotal figure in turning it from a person of noble blood into a person of moral nobility who could come from any background.
Early English translations rendered junzi as ’gentleman’; Ames and Rosemont suggested ’exemplary person’.
Ren, the broadest Confucian virtue, is translated benevolence, humaneness or goodness; the Analects defines it as ’caring for others’ (12.22).
Before Confucius, ren referred to the aristocracy of bloodlines, something like the strong and handsome look of an aristocrat; in the Analects it is a moral excellence anyone can achieve.
Li, ritual propriety, covers the conventions of ritual and etiquette, down to what to wear; asked about ren, Confucius spoke of overcoming oneself and returning to ritual propriety (12.1).
Confucius said he could not bear ritual without reverence or mourning without grief, and that at funerals the mourners’ distress matters more than the formalities.

The Mohists, followers of Mozi, argued that lavish funerals and lengthy mourning, customs the Confucians promoted, bring poverty, a smaller population and disorder, so are not what a benevolent person would do.

title: The Dao and wu wei
description: The Daodejing, credited to Laozi, teaches the Dao (the Way) and wu wei, acting without forcing, modelled on water; Zhuangzi’s Butcher Ding shows it in practice, and Confucians such as Xunzi pushed back.

facts.text: Laozi, the ’Old Master’, is said by Chinese sources to have lived in the 6th century BCE and to have written the Daodejing, but some modern scholars think he is entirely legendary.
Dao means ’way’: the Chinese graph suggests a path, and the word came to mean the right course.
The Daodejing opens, in James Legge’s translation: ’The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.’
Wu wei, often translated ’non-action’ or ’effortless action’, does not mean total inaction; in the Daodejing it contrasts with action driven by self-serving desire.

The Daodejing compares the highest excellence to water, which benefits all things without striving and takes the low place people dislike, and says nothing is softer than water yet nothing beats it at attacking the hard and strong.

In the Zhuangzi, Butcher Ding carves oxen by steering his blade through the natural gaps between the joints, so his knife is still sharp after 19 years, while a good cook changes knives every year and a mediocre one every month.
Zhuangzi, a later Daoist philosopher, lived in the 300s BCE; the IEP dates him about 369-298 BCE.
The Daodejing (ch. 38) says ritual propriety appears only after the Dao is lost, calling it a thin form of loyalty and good faith and the beginning of disorder.
The Confucian Xunzi criticized Zhuangzi as valuing nature so highly that he failed to see the value of the human.

title: The no-self argument
description: Buddhist philosophers argued that a person is a name for five changing aggregates with no lasting self behind them, as Nagasena showed King Milinda with the chariot; Nyaya critics replied that memory needs an enduring self.

facts.text: The Buddha’s teaching of non-self (anatman) denies that any of the elements making up a person is a self, and classical Indian philosophers understood him to deny the self altogether.
Buddhist thought treats a person as five kinds of aggregates (skandhas): body, feelings, perceptions, volitions and consciousness.
Buddhist philosophers held that all these elements are impermanent, so none of them can be the lasting self.
The Questions of King Milinda records a dialogue between the Buddhist monk Nagasena and King Milinda, usually identified with the Indo-Greek king Menander I (about 150 BCE).
Nagasena tells the king that ’Nagasena’ is only a designation in common use, with no permanent self behind it; the king retorts that then Nagasena is a mere empty sound and he has spoken a falsehood.

Nagasena asks whether the chariot is the pole, the axle, the wheels or other parts, all of them together, or something outside them; the king says no each time, then agrees ’chariot’ is a name used on account of the parts.
Buddhist philosophers call a chariot conventionally real: a convenient single name for its parts assembled the right way, not something over and above them; a person is the same.

Nyaya philosophers Vatsyayana and Uddyotakara objected that if I were a different self from yesterday’s ’me’, I could not remember what that ’me’ experienced; Buddhists replied that causal links within one stream of events are enough.

title: India’s schools of philosophy
description: Classical Indian schools gave rival answers: Nyaya’s logic of inference (smoke and fire), Advaita Vedanta’s identity of self and Brahman, Carvaka materialism trusting perception alone, and the Jain view that truth is many-sided.

facts.text: The oldest surviving Nyaya text is the Nyaya-sutra attributed to Gautama (about 200 CE).
Nyaya accepts four means of knowledge (pramanas): perception, inference, comparison and testimony.
Nyaya’s model inference: the hill has fire, because it has smoke, and wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen hearth and unlike a lake.

Advaita (’non-dual’) Vedanta, promoted by Shankara, who probably lived in the 8th century, holds that Brahman is the fundamental reality under everything and that the individual self is in reality identical with it, its separateness an illusion.
The Carvaka (Lokayata) materialists accepted perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge, rejecting testimony and inferences about what cannot be experienced.
The Carvakas held that consciousness is a product of the material body.

Jain philosophers hold that reality is many-sided (anekanta), so no single view captures the whole truth, an idea illustrated by the story of blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it differently.

title: Greek, Chinese and Indian beginnings
description: Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live in different ways: Plato and Aristotle on Forms and form, Chinese thinkers on how to live and govern, Indian schools on the self.

facts.text: Early Chinese philosophy addressed rulers as well as individuals: training in li was part of preparing rulers and officials, and the Daodejing says that when the sage governs through non-action, good order is universal (ch. 3).
Classical Indian schools disagreed sharply about the self: Buddhist philosophers denied a lasting self, Nyaya defended an enduring self, and Advaita Vedanta identified the self with Brahman.

title: Avicenna’s floating man
description: Avicenna imagined a man created in midair with no sensations and argued he would still affirm his own existence, so the self is known without the body; critics reply that knowing A without knowing B doesn't show A and B differ.

facts.text: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), who died in 1037, was the preeminent philosopher and physician of the Islamic world.
In his work on the soul, Avicenna asks us to suppose a man created all at once and fully formed, sight veiled, hovering in air without feeling it, limbs held apart so they don’t touch.
Avicenna held the floating man would not doubt that his self exists, while affirming no limb or organ, not his heart or brain, and no length, width or depth for that self.
Avicenna concluded that the self one is aware of is not a bodily thing known through the senses: self-awareness needs no sensory awareness of the body.
Critics, as Jari Kaukua puts the worry, say the argument slides from what the man knows to what he is: one can affirm Cicero exists without affirming Tully does, so the soul might still be the body.

title: Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd on causes
description: In the Incoherence of the Philosophers al-Ghazali denied the philosophers had proved their teachings and argued we never observe fire causing cotton to burn; Ibn Rushd’s Incoherence of the Incoherence defended real causal powers, since denying causes means denying knowledge.

facts.text: Al-Ghazali (died 1111), a leading Sunni thinker, examined twenty philosophers’ teachings in The Incoherence of the Philosophers, arguing their proofs fell short of the demonstration they demanded.
The longest discussion in al-Ghazali’s Incoherence attacks the philosophers’ claim, from Avicenna and al-Farabi, that the world has always existed; he denies it can be demonstrated.
Al-Ghazali argued that observing fire touching cotton shows only that burning occurs together with the touch, not through it; the link is not necessary, as fire without burning is conceivable.
On one account al-Ghazali offered, God creates the burning of the cotton each time, following a habit; fire, being inanimate, has no action of its own.
Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126-1198), a philosopher and physician born in Cordoba, answered al-Ghazali in The Incoherence of the Incoherence.
Ibn Rushd replied that fire keeps its power to burn even though something such as talc may hinder its action.
Ibn Rushd held that every event has four causes (agent, form, matter, end) and that denying causes denies knowledge, since intelligence perceives things with their causes.

title: Maimonides and negative theology
description: Maimonides’s Guide for the Perplexed read the Bible’s bodily language about God non-literally to fit it with Aristotle’s philosophy, held that neither creation nor eternity can be demonstrated, and argued we can say only what God is not.

facts.text: Moses Maimonides (1138-1204) was born in Cordoba and spent much of his adult life in Fustat, near Cairo.
Maimonides’s Guide for the Perplexed (Guide of the Perplexed), completed in 1190, is framed as a letter to an advanced student torn between philosophy and his religion’s teachings.
Maimonides held that biblical terms that seem to give God bodily qualities must not be read literally, since literal reading leads to a material conception of God.

Against the Aristotelian view that the world is eternal, Maimonides argued that neither the eternity of the world nor its creation can be demonstrated, and judged creation the better-supported belief.
Maimonides held God is one, without parts or separate attributes, and comparable to nothing, so ‘God is powerful’ should be read as ‘God does not lack power’.
Maimonides wrote that the more you can prove inapplicable to God the better, and concluded that the highest praise of God is silence.
The Guide was controversial and at first banned in some rabbinic circles; critics asked whether its reading of the Torah owed more to Aristotle and al-Farabi than to Moses.

title: Aquinas on faith and reason
description: Thomas Aquinas reworked Aristotle within Christian theology and held that reason can reach some truths about God while others need revelation; since faith goes beyond reason but never against it, a clash means reasoning has failed.

facts.text: In the medieval university, the arts faculty’s curriculum consisted largely of the works of Aristotle.
Thomas Aquinas (about 1225-1274), a Dominican friar who taught theology in Paris, took inspiration above all from Aristotle and built a systematic reworking of Aristotelianism.
Aquinas wrote long commentaries on Aristotle’s works, confident that progress in philosophy would only benefit the Christian faith.
Aquinas held that some truths about God, such as that God exists and is one, reason can reach without revelation (the preambles of faith), while others, such as the Trinity, need revelation.
For Aquinas, faith takes us beyond what natural reason can grasp but never contradicts what we know by natural reason.
Aquinas wrote that anything in the philosophers contrary to the faith ‘is not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy, due to a failure of reason’.
In On the Eternity of the World, Aquinas concluded that no demonstrative argument settles whether the world had a beginning; that it did is known by faith.
Aquinas rejected Maimonides’s reading of ‘God is good’ as ‘God is not evil’: saying God lives means more than that; the good in creatures pre-exists in God in a higher way.

In 1277, three years to the day after Aquinas’s death, 219 propositions were condemned in Paris, a significant number seeming to implicate his teachings; Franciscan critics published ‘corrections’ of him, and his supporters defended him.

title: Wang Yangming’s unity of knowing and acting
description: Wang Yangming, after failing to find the principle of bamboo by staring at it, held that moral principle lies in the mind and that knowing and acting are one: those who know but do not act do not yet know.

facts.text: Wang Yangming (1472-1529) was a Chinese statesman, general and Neo-Confucian philosopher, a leading critic of Zhu Xi’s orthodox Neo-Confucianism.
Trying Zhu Xi’s investigation of things, Wang’s friend Qian stared at bamboos to find their principle and fell ill on the third day; Wang tried next and fell ill on the seventh.
In exile in what is now Guizhou, Wang had a philosophical awakening in 1508: moral truth is not found by searching outside, since the principle is fully present in the mind.
Wang’s best-known doctrine is the unity of knowing and acting: ‘those who know but do not act simply do not yet know’; saying filial words doesn’t show you know filial piety.
Wang used the Great Learning’s image that hating evil is like hating a hateful odor: recognizing the smell and being repelled by it are one.
Zhu Xi, like Aristotle, would accept a plagiarist’s claim to have known it was wrong (weakness of will); critics add that finding something attractive or repellent need not lead to action.

title: Descartes’s method of doubt
description: Descartes set out to doubt every belief open to any doubt, using dreams and an all-powerful deceiver, and found that his own existence while thinking survives: “I am, I exist”, later “I think, therefore I am”.

facts.text: Descartes compared removing false beliefs to emptying a basket of apples, some rotten: tip them all out, then put back only those seen to be sound.
In the Meditations (1641), Descartes resolved to withhold assent from any opinion with even some reason for doubt, to reach a certain foundation for knowledge.
Descartes’s dream doubt: for all I know I am dreaming now, so the senses give no certainty; yet awake or asleep, two and three added together make five.
Descartes then supposed a deceiver of supreme power and cunning who could fool him even about the simplest truths.
In the Second Meditation, if a deceiver deceives me I must exist: ‘I am, I exist’ is necessarily true whenever I put it forward or conceive it.
‘I think, therefore I am’ appears in French in the Discourse on the Method (1637) and in Latin, ‘cogito, ergo sum’, in the Principles of Philosophy (1644), not in that form in the Meditations.

Pierre Gassendi, whose objections were printed with the Meditations in 1641, objected that treating everything as false and imagining a deceiving demon was excessive; Descartes replied that errors absorbed since infancy aren’t so easily removed.

title: Spinoza, Leibniz and rationalism
description: Rationalists hold that reason gives knowledge the senses can’t: Spinoza argued like geometry to one substance, “God, or Nature”, acting from necessity; Leibniz used sufficient reason to argue God chose the best of all possible worlds, a claim Voltaire mocked.

facts.text: Rationalists claim some concepts and knowledge are gained independently of sense experience; Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz are traditionally the Continental Rationalists, though the labels need caution.
Spinoza (1632-1677) of Amsterdam built his Ethics from definitions and axioms, demonstrating each proposition from what precedes it.
Spinoza argued there is only one substance, God, and everything else is in God; ‘God, or Nature’ (Deus, sive Natura) sums this up, a being acting from the same necessity by which it exists.
Leibniz (1646-1716) held the principle of sufficient reason: there must be a sufficient reason why things are as they are and not otherwise.
Leibniz argued that God, all-powerful, all-knowing and good, chose this world from infinitely many possible worlds, so it must be the best of all possible worlds.
Leibniz’s best-world thesis was roundly mocked in Voltaire’s Candide; Leibniz did not say everything in this world is wonderful.

title: Locke, Berkeley and Hume: empiricism
description: The empiricists held that all ideas come from experience: Locke’s blank slate, Berkeley’s claim that to be is to be perceived, and Hume’s ideas as copies of impressions; Leibniz replied that the mind is veined marble, not a blank slate.

facts.text: In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), Locke argued we have no innate knowledge: at birth the mind is a blank slate, and all ideas come from experience, sensation and reflection.
Berkeley held that an apple is a collection of ideas, a colour, taste, smell, figure and consistency observed together; he denied mind-independent matter, not ordinary objects.
Berkeley’s famous principle is that to be is to be perceived (esse est percipi).
Critics asked whether an unperceived tree in the Quad stops existing; one reply Berkeley suggests is that another spirit, God, always perceives it.
Hume divided perceptions into lively impressions and fainter ideas that copy them; a golden mountain just joins two ideas we already have, gold and mountain.
Hume granted that someone familiar with every shade of blue but one could probably imagine the missing shade, an exception he judged too singular to change his principle.
Against Locke’s blank slate, Leibniz’s New Essays offered a block of marble whose veins determine what figures it will accept: the mind helps determine its contents.

title: Kant’s Copernican revolution
description: Kant argued that objects must conform to our ways of knowing: the mind supplies space and time and concepts such as cause, so experience has content from the senses and form from the mind; we know only appearances, as Jacobi’s objection pressed.

facts.text: Kant (1724-1804) wrote that the remembrance of David Hume first interrupted his ‘dogmatic slumber’.
Hume argued that neither reason nor experience can justify beliefs such as ‘every event must have a cause’.
In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Kant proposed that objects conform to our cognition rather than cognition to objects, comparing this to Copernicus moving the observer instead of the stars.
For Kant, the mind supplies space and time as forms of intuition and a priori concepts such as cause, so the experienced world necessarily conforms to laws like ‘every event has a cause’.

Kant argued against empiricists that the mind is no blank slate but structures experience, and against rationalists that reason alone can’t know beyond experience: ‘Thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind.’
Kant held that we know only appearances, never things in themselves.
Jacobi objected that without the thing in itself he could not enter Kant’s system and with it could not stay, since Kant applies cause to things in themselves though he limits it to experience.

title: Avicenna to Kant: reason, faith and experience
description: From Avicenna to Kant, philosophers argued over what reason alone can know, how faith relates to reason, and whether knowledge comes from experience, with recurring debates over the self and over causes.

facts.text: An objection to Avicenna’s floating man, how we know the knowing subject is the self, may also be levelled at Descartes’s cogito.
The claim that we observe only succession, not causation, is most commonly identified with Hume but was made earlier by al-Baqillani and repeated by al-Ghazali.

title: Knowledge as justified true belief
description: The classic definition says you know something when it is true, you believe it and you are justified in believing it; the justification condition is there to rule out lucky guesses.

facts.text: The traditional (tripartite) analysis says S knows that P if and only if P is true, S believes P and S is justified in believing P; it is abbreviated JTB, justified true belief.
Most epistemologists agree that what is false cannot be known: eighty-four is not prime, so nobody can know that it is; truth is a matter of how things are, not how they can be shown to be.
The belief condition says you can only know what you believe: failing to believe something precludes knowing it. Knowledge is a kind of relationship with the truth.
Justification is added to rule out lucky guesses: someone who confidently believes a coin will land tails on no basis is right by luck, and that can’t count as knowledge.

In Plato’s Theaetetus (200d-201c) Socrates argues that true belief is not knowledge: a skilled lawyer can bring jurymen to a true belief without knowledge. The need for justification is often traced to this.
Crispin Sartwell (1991, 1992) argued that knowledge is merely true belief and justification is not needed; it is a heterodox view that most epistemologists reject.

title: The Gettier problem
description: Edmund Gettier’s 1963 cases show a justified true belief made true by luck, which almost all epistemologists agree is not knowledge, so the three-part definition falls short.

facts.text: Edmund Gettier’s 1963 article ‘Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?’ gave cases of beliefs that are true and well justified yet, almost all epistemologists agree, are not knowledge.

Gettier’s Case I: Smith and Jones applied for a job; the company president told Smith Jones would get it, and Smith counted ten coins in Jones’s pocket, so he inferred the man who gets the job has ten coins in his pocket.
In Case I Smith himself gets the job and, unknown to him, has ten coins in his own pocket; his belief is true, believed and justified, but true by luck, so it is not knowledge.
Gettier’s article had a dramatic impact: almost all epistemologists agreed he had refuted the traditional definition, and many tried to add a fourth condition to JTB.

One proposed fix is that a known belief must not be inferred from any falsehood (Smith relied on the false belief that Jones would get the job); it is not widely accepted, as Gettier cases need not involve false evidence.
Roderick Chisholm’s sheep in the field: you see what looks exactly like a sheep, really a disguised dog, and believe a sheep is in the field; you are right, as one is hidden behind a hill.

title: The ancient Pyrrhonian skeptics
description: Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus set equal and opposing arguments against each other, suspended judgment and found tranquillity; critics said they could not act without beliefs.

facts.text: Pyrrho of Elis lived from about 365-360 BCE to about 275-270 BCE and wrote nothing; his philosophy is reconstructed from reports by others.
Sextus Empiricus, probably of the 2nd or 3rd century CE, wrote the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, the best and fullest account of Pyrrhonian skepticism, named after Pyrrho.
The Pyrrhonian skeptic’s skill is finding for every argument an equal and opposing argument, which brings suspension of judgment (epoche) and ultimately tranquillity.
Skeptics used phrases such as ‘No more this than that’ and ‘I determine nothing’ to express their suspension of judgment.
Sextus compares skeptical tranquillity to the painter Apelles, who failed to paint a horse’s foam, flung his sponge at the picture in frustration, and so produced the foam.
The most widely discussed objection to the ancient skeptics is the apraxia charge: that they cannot act without belief. They replied that they act guided by appearances.
Sextus says the skeptic lives by appearances: by nature’s guidance (perceiving and thinking), by feelings (hunger leads to food), by handed-down customs and laws, and by teaching of skills.

title: The brain in a vat
description: The skeptic says you cannot know you are not a brain in a vat; Hilary Putnam argued that, since words refer only through causal links, the thought “we are brains in a vat” refutes itself.

facts.text: Brain in a vat: imagine you are a brain hooked to a computer that perfectly simulates experience. Skeptic: if I know P (say, snow is white) I know I am not a brain in a vat; I don’t know that; so I don’t know P.
The brain-in-a-vat argument is usually taken as a modern version of Descartes’s evil demon, who systematically deceives us.
Hilary Putnam’s Reason, Truth and History (1981) opens with an ant that by chance traces a line like a caricature of Winston Churchill; it has not depicted Churchill, having never seen him.
Putnam’s causal constraint: a term refers to an object only if there is an appropriate causal connection between the term and the object.

Putnam supposed all sentient beings are brains in a vat run by a computer with no programmer; their ‘vat’ is not causally linked to vats, so ‘We are brains in a vat’ is self-refuting, like ‘All general statements are false’.
Crispin Wright (1994) argued that Putnam’s argument leaves some versions untouched, such as my brain being taken out last night and hooked up to a computer.

title: A priori and a posteriori knowledge
description: A priori knowledge is knowable independently of experience, by reason alone; a posteriori knowledge rests on experience. Mill argued that even arithmetic is learned from experience.

facts.text: A proposition is knowable a priori if it can be known independently of any experience other than learning the language; a posteriori if known on the basis of experience. ‘All bachelors are unmarried’ vs ‘it is raining outside’.
A priori examples: cubes have six sides; if today is Tuesday then today is not Thursday; seven plus five equals twelve. A posteriori: water is H2O; dinosaurs existed.
Once the terms are understood, a priori truths seem visible just by reflecting on their content, so a priori justification is described as coming from pure thought or reason.
John Stuart Mill held that even the laws of arithmetic and geometry are learned by inductive reasoning from experience.
Critics such as A. J. Ayer replied that Mill’s view makes statements like ‘2 + 2 = 4’ uncertain, contingent truths.

title: Hume's problem of induction
description: Hume argued that no argument can show the future will resemble the past without assuming it; he traced our expectations to custom, and Reichenbach later offered a pragmatic vindication.

facts.text: Hume, Enquiry (1748): ‘That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.’
Hume: the bread he formerly ate nourished him, but does it follow that other bread must nourish him at another time? ‘The consequence seems nowise necessary.’

Hume’s dilemma: an argument that the future resembles the past is demonstrative or probable; not demonstrative, since nature changing implies no contradiction; a probable one assumes it, ‘taking that for granted, which is the very point in question’.

Hume did not deny we draw such inferences; he traced them to custom or habit: having seen flame and heat conjoined, the mind is carried by custom to expect heat. ‘Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.’

Hans Reichenbach accepted Hume’s argument but offered a pragmatic vindication: induction works if any method works, like a physician who says that if any remedy will save the patient, it is the operation.

title: Nyaya's means of knowledge
description: Nyaya’s four pramanas are perception, inference, comparison and testimony; its five-step inference rests on a pervasion such as smoke never without fire, which the Carvakas doubted.

facts.text: Nyaya calls perception the ‘eldest’ means of knowledge, since the other pramanas depend on perceptual input.
Nyaya defines testimony as the assertion of a qualified speaker: one with direct knowledge and willing to convey it without distortion.
Nyaya’s stock example of comparison: a person told that a water buffalo looks like a cow later sees such an animal and recognizes it; it is mainly used for learning what words refer to.

Nyaya’s five-step inference: fire on the hill (thesis); because smoke is on it (reason); wherever smoke, fire, like a kitchen hearth, unlike a lake (example); this hill is smoky (application); so fire (conclusion).
The pervasion (vyapti), ‘wherever there is smoke there is fire’, grounds the inference: fire pervades smoke, as we never find smoke without fire.
The Carvakas rejected inference as a source of knowledge because it depends on generalizations that outstrip perceptual evidence; no one can know that every F is a G.

The standard reply to the Carvaka was pragmatic: we could not act as we do without relying on inference, and the skeptic relies on generalizations whenever he speaks, using words with repeatable meanings.

title: Correspondence and coherence theories of truth
description: The correspondence theory says a belief is true when it matches the world; the coherence theory says it is true when it fits with other beliefs. Each faces a classic objection.

facts.text: The correspondence theory is often traced to Aristotle, Metaphysics 1011b25: ‘To say of what is that it is not, or of what is not that it is, is false, while to say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true’.
The correspondence theory says a proposition is true if and only if it corresponds to a fact, a way the world is.
A coherence theory of truth says a proposition is true if and only if it coheres with some specified set of propositions, often a set of beliefs.

Coherence shows how we arrive at truth claims: a drunk driver’s report of pink elephants on the highway is rejected as false because it fails to cohere with other beliefs (elephants are gray, no zoo or circus nearby, nobody else sees them).
A popular objection to correspondence: we cannot step outside our own minds to compare our thoughts with mind-independent reality, so on that theory knowledge would be impossible.
Coherence theories were adopted by British Idealists around 1900, such as F. H. Bradley.

Russell’s 1907 objection: ‘Jane Austen was hanged for murder’ coheres with some set of propositions, as ‘Jane Austen died in her bed’ does with another. Coherentists reply truth is coherence with what is actually believed.

title: Pragmatism about meaning and truth
description: The American pragmatists Peirce, James and Dewey tied meaning and truth to practical consequences: Peirce’s maxim, truth as the end of inquiry, James’s expedient belief, Dewey’s inquiry as problem solving.

facts.text: Pragmatism originated in the United States around 1870 with Charles Sanders Peirce and William James; John Dewey led its second generation.

Peirce’s pragmatic maxim (1878, ‘How to Make Our Ideas Clear’): consider the practical effects we conceive the object of our conception to have; our conception of those effects is our whole conception of the object.
Peirce’s first example: what we mean by calling a thing hard is that it will not be scratched by many other substances.
Peirce: ‘The opinion which is fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate, is what we mean by the truth’; hence the slogan that truth is the end (goal) of inquiry.

William James, Pragmatism (1907): ‘The true … is only the expedient in the way of our thinking’, in the long run and on the whole; ideas become true as they help us into satisfactory relation with our experience.
John Dewey saw inquiry as beginning with a problem and aiming to resolve it; the logical forms used in inquiry are instruments, tools that help resolve the problem.

Russell (1946) objected that James is committed to the truth of ‘Santa Claus exists’; James’s defenders call this unfair, since a comforting belief is wholly true only if it does not clash with other vital benefits.

title: Answering the skeptic
description: Philosophers answer doubt about knowledge in different ways: suspending judgment, calling the doubt self-refuting, relying on custom or practice, or, like Peirce, refusing to fake doubt while accepting fallibilism.

facts.text: Peirce (1868) rejected doubting all beliefs at once: ‘Let us not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts’; real doubt needs a positive reason.
Peirce insisted on fallibilism: at any point inquiry is provisional and we cannot tell how far we are from the truth, yet he was no sceptic about answering genuine questions.
The attempt to analyze knowledge got much attention, especially in the late 20th century, but no analysis has been widely accepted; some epistemologists deny knowledge can be analyzed.

title: The mind-body problem
description: The mind-body problem asks how thoughts and feelings relate to the physical body: what minds and bodies are, and how each affects the other; dualism, materialism and idealism are the classic answers.

facts.text: People seem to have physical properties, such as size, weight, shape and motion, and also mental properties, such as perceptions, emotions, beliefs and desires, which we don’t attribute to typical physical objects.
The mind-body problem is the problem of explaining how mind and body relate: how one being can have such different mental and physical characteristics, when mind and body seem to interact closely.

The mind-body problem includes an ontological question (what are mind and body, and is one nothing over and above the other?) and a causal question (do physical states influence mental states, and mental states physical ones, and if so, how?).
The classic interaction puzzle asks how the mind can make a limb move, as when you raise your hand to ask a question, and how the body’s sense organs can cause sensations in the mind.

The three classic answers to the mind-body problem are dualism (mind and body are both real and fundamentally distinct), materialism, also called physicalism (the mind is fundamentally physical), and idealism (matter is fundamentally mental).

title: Descartes’s dualism and its critics
description: Descartes held that the mind is a thinking, unextended thing distinct from the extended body; Princess Elisabeth asked how such a mind could move a body, and Ryle called the view the ghost in the machine, a category mistake.

facts.text: Descartes argued that the mind is a thinking, non-extended thing and the body an extended, non-thinking thing, so the two are really distinct and one could exist without the other; the view is now called mind-body dualism.
In the Sixth Meditation Descartes argued that the body is always divisible while the mind is utterly indivisible, since he could find no parts in himself as a thinking thing.
In 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia began her correspondence with Descartes by asking how the soul, being only a thinking thing, can move the body to produce voluntary actions.

Elisabeth’s worry, shared by Gassendi: to set something in motion, a thing must come into contact with it, like one pool ball striking another, but a mind with no extension has no surface to touch the body with.
In The Concept of Mind (1949), Gilbert Ryle called the dualist picture of the mind, “with deliberate abusiveness”, “the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine”.
Ryle argued that the dogma is a category mistake: it presents the facts of mental life as if they belonged to one logical category, when they belong to another.
Ryle’s example: a visitor shown the colleges, libraries and offices of Oxford or Cambridge asks, “But where is the University?”, not seeing that the University is just the way all of it is organized.
Ryle said he was not denying that mental processes occur: doing long division is a mental process, and so is making a joke.

title: The mind-brain identity theory
description: The identity theory of Place, Feigl and Smart holds that each mental state just is a brain state, as lightning is an electrical discharge; Putnam objected that pain is multiply realized.

facts.text: The identity theory holds that mental states and processes, such as an experience of pain, just are brain processes, not merely correlated with them; it is a form of physicalism.
The identity theory took shape in U.T. Place’s 1956 paper “Is Consciousness a Brain Process?” and in work by Herbert Feigl and J.J.C. Smart in the late 1950s.
Place compared “consciousness is a brain process” to “lightning is a motion of electric charges”: the two words differ in meaning, and we find each out differently, yet they pick out the same thing.
Identity theorists treat “sensations are brain processes” as a truth we had to find out, not a matter of definition; after all, Aristotle thought the brain was for cooling the blood.

In 1967 Hilary Putnam objected that many creatures, from mammals and birds to mollusks such as octopuses, seem able to feel pain with very different brains, so pain can’t be identical to one kind of brain state.
David Lewis replied that such identities are specific to a kind of creature: pain can be one brain state in human nervous systems and another in mollusk nervous systems.

title: Functionalism
description: Functionalism defines a mental state by the role it plays between inputs, other mental states and behavior, not by what it is made of, so minds could in principle run on silicon; Block’s Chinese nation challenges it.

facts.text: Functionalism holds that what makes something a mental state, such as pain, depends not on what it is made of but on its function: its causal relations to sensory input, other mental states and behavior.
A key is anything that can open the lock, whether metal, wood or plastic; functionalists say mental states are like keys, identified by what they do rather than what they are made of.
A simple functionalist theory defines pain as the state caused by bodily injury that produces the belief that something is wrong, the desire to be out of that state, anxiety, and wincing or moaning.
On functionalism, pain could be C-fiber stimulation in humans and a silicon-based state in a hypothetical Martian or android, as long as each plays pain’s role.

Hilary Putnam modeled mental states on computing machines, where a program fixes how inputs and internal states lead to outputs, and defended functionalism as a theory in a 1967 paper; the comparison of minds with computers is only an analogy.

Ned Block’s Chinese nation case imagines the population of China duplicating a brain’s functional organization, each person acting like a neuron; Block argues the system would have no experiences, while Daniel Dennett replied that such cases only trouble crude functional theories.

title: Turing’s imitation game
description: Turing (1950) replaced “Can machines think?” with a game in which a machine’s typed answers try to fool an interrogator; objections ask whether passing shows thought or feeling.

facts.text: In his 1950 paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, Alan Turing set out to replace the question “Can machines think?”, which he called “too meaningless to deserve discussion”, with a game.

In Turing’s imitation game an interrogator in a separate room puts questions to two hidden players and gets typewritten answers, so tone of voice can’t help; first the task is to tell the man from the woman, then a machine takes a player’s place.

Turing predicted that in about 50 years computers could play the imitation game so well that an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 percent chance of a right identification after five minutes of questioning.

Turing answered the “argument from consciousness”, from Professor Jefferson’s 1949 lecture, that a machine must feel its thoughts, not merely produce symbols; he replied that we can’t be sure anyone else thinks, yet keep “the polite convention that everyone thinks”.

Ned Block’s “Blockhead” is run by a vast look-up tree holding a programmed reply for every input; it could answer just as you would, and critics take it to show that passing the Turing Test isn’t enough for intelligence.

title: Searle’s Chinese room
description: Searle’s 1980 Chinese room argues that manipulating symbols by rules is not understanding them, so running a program cannot by itself produce understanding; the systems reply says the whole system understands.

facts.text: John Searle published the Chinese room argument in 1980, in “Minds, Brains and Programs” in the journal Behavioral and Brain Sciences.

Searle imagines himself alone in a room, following a program written in English for answering Chinese characters slipped under the door; he understands no Chinese, yet his replies lead people outside to think a Chinese speaker is inside.

Searle’s point: a computer only manipulates symbols by their syntax, without grasping their meaning (semantics), so running a program can’t by itself produce understanding, and the Turing Test is inadequate.

The argument targets what Searle calls Strong AI, the view that a suitably programmed computer really understands; Searle says brains are machines and brains think, so he isn’t claiming no machine can think.
The systems reply, which Searle called perhaps the most common, grants that the man doesn’t understand Chinese but says the whole system, man plus instructions plus memory, does.
Searle answered that he could memorize the instructions and do everything in his head, becoming the whole system, and still not understand Chinese.

title: Nagel’s bat
description: Nagel (1974) held that a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be it, and argued that an objective physical theory may leave out that subjective point of view.

facts.text: In “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” (1974), Thomas Nagel held that an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism, for the organism: the subjective character of experience.
Nagel chose bats because most perceive the world mainly by sonar, the echoes of their own high-pitched shrieks, a sense unlike any of ours.
Nagel said that imagining webbed arms, poor eyesight and hanging upside down in an attic only tells you what it would be like for you to behave like a bat, not what it is like for a bat to be a bat.
Nagel argued that every subjective experience is tied to a single point of view, while an objective, physical theory seems bound to abandon that point of view.
Nagel said it would be a mistake to conclude that physicalism is false; rather, we don’t yet have any idea how it could be true.
Kathleen Akins studied bat physiology and argued that many questions about a bat’s experience that seem open depend on neuroscientific details we haven’t yet worked out.

title: Mary’s room
description: Jackson’s Mary knows every physical fact about color vision but has never seen color; if she learns something on release, not all information is physical, while the ability hypothesis says she gains only know-how.

facts.text: In Frank Jackson’s 1982 thought experiment, Mary, a brilliant scientist in a black and white room with a black and white television, learns all the physical information about seeing colors, such as which wavelengths stimulate the retina and how this leads to saying “The sky is blue”.

Jackson asked whether Mary learns anything when she is released; it seems obvious she does, so her physical knowledge was incomplete, and he concluded that not all information is physical and physicalism is false.
The ability hypothesis, defended by David Lewis and Laurence Nemirow, says Mary gains no new facts on release, only abilities, such as to imagine, remember and recognize colors.
Jackson later changed his mind: he came to argue that something must be wrong with the knowledge argument, and now defends physicalism, though others still defend the argument.

title: The hard problem of consciousness
description: Chalmers (1995) separated the easy problems of explaining brain functions from the hard problem of why they come with experience; the Churchlands replied that neuroscience makes the gap hard to imagine.

facts.text: David Chalmers named the hard problem of consciousness in “Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness”, published in the Journal of Consciousness Studies in 1995.

Chalmers’s easy problems include explaining how we discriminate and react to stimuli, integrate information, report our mental states, focus attention, control behavior and differ between waking and sleep.
Chalmers said “easy” is relative: the easy problems may take a century or two of difficult empirical work, but the methods of cognitive science and neuroscience should succeed.
The hard problem is the problem of experience: why all this information processing comes with a subjective inner life, such as the quality of deep blue or the sensation of middle C.

Chalmers argued that the hard problem is not a problem about performing functions, so the standard methods for explaining functions leave it standing even when every relevant function has been explained.
Paul and Patricia Churchland replied that the more one learns about how the brain produces experience, the harder it becomes to imagine creatures with brain processes like ours but no consciousness.

title: Theories of mind compared
description: Dualism, the identity theory and functionalism each answer the mind-body problem and each faces its own objection, while consciousness puzzles challenge physical theories in general.

facts.text: In a 2020 survey of professional philosophers (Bourget and Chalmers), 22% accepted or leaned toward dualism as a response to the mind-body problem, and 51% toward materialism.

The identity theory is a form of physicalism, and functionalism is compatible with it too, but functionalism is more inclusive: it lets creatures with brains unlike ours, or no brains, share our mental states.

title: Moral relativism
description: Moral relativism holds that moral truth is relative to a culture, as Herodotus’s story of opposite funeral customs suggests; critics reply that it makes reform and moral progress impossible to judge.

facts.text: Herodotus tells how the Persian king Darius asked Greeks what price would make them eat their dead fathers (none, they said), then asked the Callatians of India, who ate their dead parents, what would make them burn their fathers; they cried out and told him to stop.
Herodotus concluded that every people would choose its own customs as the best, and approved the poet Pindar’s saying that custom is lord (king) of all.
Moral relativism is the view that moral truth or justification is relative to a culture or society; relativists hold that no attempt to prove one moral outlook objectively correct succeeds.

Critics’ most serious objection is that relativism implies ‘anything goes’: slavery counts as just in a slave society, a culture’s own norms can’t be criticized, and moral progress such as abolishing slavery becomes impossible to call progress.
Relativists commonly reply that moral progress can still be judged, but only from a particular moral standpoint rather than from an objective ‘God’s-eye’ point of view.

Around the time Herodotus wrote, the Mohists pointed to far-off peoples whose customs Chinese readers found barbaric, and argued that a practice’s being customary does not make it right, so their own customs could be wrong too.

title: The Euthyphro dilemma
description: Plato’s Euthyphro asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious or pious because loved; restated for God, one horn makes morality arbitrary and the other makes it independent of God.

facts.text: In Plato’s Euthyphro, Socrates, on his way to answer the charges against him, meets Euthyphro at the court; Euthyphro is prosecuting his own father over the death of a laborer and claims special knowledge of piety.
Socrates rejects Euthyphro’s own case as a definition of piety and asks instead for the one idea that makes every pious thing pious, a standard to measure actions by.
When Euthyphro says piety is what all the gods love, Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved.
Philosophers restate the dilemma for God and morality: does God command an action because it is morally right, or is it morally right because God commands it?

If an act is right because God commands it, morality looks arbitrary (had God commanded cruelty for fun, it would be right); if God commands it because it is right, rightness is independent of God, who recognizes morality rather than creating it.

Robert Adams’s modified divine command theory holds that an act is wrong if and only if it is contrary to the commands of a loving God, so morality rests on God’s unchanging good nature and cruelty for its own sake could not be commanded.
Critics reply that taking God’s character as the standard of goodness still seems arbitrary unless that character measures up to some standard of goodness itself.

title: Glaucon’s challenge
description: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon argues that people value justice only for its rewards and challenges Socrates to show that justice is good in itself, even stripped of reputation.

facts.text: In Book II of the Republic, Glaucon says he is not himself of the opinion that injustice is better, but he has never heard justice defended satisfactorily, so he argues the other side.

Glaucon divides goods into three classes: those welcomed for their own sake, like harmless pleasures; those good in themselves and for their results, like knowledge, sight and health; and those chosen only for their results, like exercise, medical treatment and money-making.
Socrates places justice in the class of goods valued both for their own sake and for their results; Glaucon says most people put it among the burdensome goods pursued only for rewards and reputation.

Glaucon states the common view that people, having done and suffered injustice, agree to have neither, making laws; justice is a compromise between the best, doing injustice unpunished, and the worst, suffering it without retaliation.

Glaucon asks us to compare a perfectly unjust man with the greatest reputation for justice and a perfectly just man thought the worst of men all his life, stripped of reputation so we see whether he is just for justice’s sake or for rewards, and to judge which is happier.

Glaucon asks Socrates to set aside rewards and results and show what justice does, in itself, to the soul of the person who has it; his brother Adeimantus adds ‘whether seen or unseen by gods and men’. The rest of the Republic answers this challenge.

title: Mencius and Xunzi on human nature
description: Mencius held that people are born with sprouts of goodness that must be extended; Xunzi held that human nature is bad and goodness is built by artifice, teachers and ritual.

facts.text: Mencius, a Confucian of the fourth century BCE, argued that anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well would feel alarm and compassion, not to win favor with the parents, gain praise from neighbors or escape the child’s cries.

Mencius held that every heart has four sprouts: sympathy, shame, deference to others, and approving and condemning, which are the sprouts of ren (humaneness), rightness, li (ritual propriety) and wisdom.
For Mencius the sprouts are incipient, not fully formed virtues, and must be extended: a king who spared an ox from slaughter was urged to extend the same compassion to his suffering people.

Xunzi’s chapter “Human Nature Is Evil” (the word e is close to ‘detestable’) says people are born fond of profit, and following it leads to contention and robbery; what is good in people is artifice (wei), traits acquired by conscious effort through teachers and ritual.
Xunzi compared reforming human nature to a potter making a pot from clay and to straightening bent wood with a press-frame: without the craftsman, neither happens on its own.

Both Mencius and Xunzi held that everyone can become good with great effort; they differed over where the guide lies, Mencius looking inward to the heart and Xunzi outward to the rituals handed down by the sages, the best guide for most people.

title: Aristotle’s golden mean
description: Aristotle held that each virtue is a mean between excess and deficiency, relative to the person, and that virtues are built by practice, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness.

facts.text: For Aristotle each virtue is a mean between a vice of excess and one of deficiency: courage lies between cowardice, fleeing every danger with too much fear, and rashness, facing every danger with little or no fear.

Aristotle’s mean is relative to us, not an arithmetic middle: if 10 pounds of food is too much and 2 too little, a trainer won’t order 6, which would be too little for Milo the athlete and too much for a beginner.
Aristotle holds that some actions, such as theft and murder, have no mean and are always wrong.

Aristotle argued that we acquire virtues by practice, as people become builders by building and harp-players by playing the harp: by doing just acts we become just, and by doing brave acts, brave; lawgivers make citizens good by habituation.
A common criticism of virtue ethics is that it answers “What sort of person should I be?” but not “What should I do?”, so it cannot guide action.

Rosalind Hursthouse replied that virtue and vice words give specific guidance, such as “do what is honest or charitable; do not do what is dishonest”, and that the list of vice words is remarkably long.

title: Utilitarianism
description: Bentham judged actions by their tendency to promote pleasure and prevent pain; Mill added that some pleasures are higher in kind; critics say the sum can overlook justice and rights.

facts.text: Jeremy Bentham (1748 to 1832), in An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), held that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.

Bentham’s principle of utility approves actions, by governments and individuals alike, that tend to promote happiness and disapproves those that tend to cause pain; Bentham and Mill attacked traditions defended as the natural order, appealing to utility instead.
Bentham measured pleasures by quantity: intensity, duration, certainty, nearness, fruitfulness, purity and extent; on this basis studying for an exam can beat going to a party.
Critics attacked the pleasure-based view as a morality fit only for swine; Mill’s distinction between higher and lower pleasures was offered in answer to that charge against Bentham’s view.
In Utilitarianism (1861), Mill held that actions are right as they tend to promote happiness, that intellectual pleasures are higher in kind, and that people who know both kinds prefer the higher.
Mill wrote: “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.”

A common objection is that utilitarianism seems to overlook justice and rights, since adding up happiness could approve sacrificing one innocent person for many; some utilitarians accept such verdicts, while most modify the theory.

title: Kant’s categorical imperative
description: Kant’s categorical imperative commands unconditionally: act only on maxims you could will as universal law, and never treat humanity merely as a means, as a false promise does.

facts.text: Kant distinguished hypothetical imperatives, which command an action as good for some purpose, from the categorical imperative, which declares an action necessary in itself without reference to any purpose; moral duty is categorical.
In Abbott’s translation, Kant’s categorical imperative reads: “Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.”

Kant tests the maxim of borrowing money with a promise to repay that one knows one can’t keep: made universal, the promise itself would become impossible, since no one would believe it and people would ridicule such statements as vain pretences.

Another form of the categorical imperative says to treat humanity, in your own person or anyone else’s, always as an end and never as a means only; the lying promiser uses the lender merely as a means, in a way the lender could not assent to.
The humanity formula does not forbid using people as means, only using them merely as means: we may use a taxi driver to get somewhere, provided his humanity is at the same time treated as an end.

In Utilitarianism, Mill wrote that when Kant derives actual duties he fails ‘almost grotesquely’ to show any contradiction in universally adopting immoral rules: “All he shows is that the consequences of their universal adoption would be such as no one would choose to incur.”
Kantians reply that the contradiction is real: a lying promise needs a practice of taking people’s word, which the universalized maxim would abolish.

title: The ethics of care
description: Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings developed an ethics that starts from caring relationships rather than universal rules; critics call it a slave morality or parochial.

facts.text: Lawrence Kohlberg’s model saw moral development moving toward universal principles, and girls scored lower; Carol Gilligan, whose mentor he was, argued his model was biased and heard a ‘different voice’ of care in In a Different Voice (1982).

On Kohlberg’s Heinz dilemma (steal a drug he can’t afford to save his wife?), Gilligan’s Jake, 11, saw a math problem with people, life outranking property; Amy, 11, said no, as jail could leave the wife worse off, and saw relationships to talk through to find the money.

In Caring (1984), Nel Noddings described caring relationships between the one-caring and the cared-for, caring as engrossment (receiving the other on their own terms), and rejected universal principles for prescribed action.

Critics call care ethics a slave morality (Nietzsche’s term) that praises traits shaped by women’s oppression, and parochial for favoring those nearby over distant others; Noddings later endorsed a stronger obligation to care about distant people.
Care ethics is typically contrasted with Kantian and utilitarian ethics; care ethicists object that Kantian ethics proceeds from absolute, universal principles.

title: Hume’s is and ought
description: Hume argued that an ought expresses a new relation that cannot simply be deduced from claims about what is; Philippa Foot’s naturalism challenges the gap.

facts.text: Hume’s A Treatise of Human Nature was published in 1739 and 1740.

Hume noticed that authors on morality reason for a while with ‘is’ and ‘is not’, about God or human affairs, then suddenly connect every proposition with ‘ought’ or ‘ought not’, a change he called imperceptible but ‘of the last consequence’.
Hume argued that an ‘ought’ expresses a new relation, so a reason must be given for how it can be deduced from other claims entirely different from it.
On the dominant twentieth-century reading, Hume holds that no ought-conclusion can be validly inferred from premises that only state what is; R. M. Hare and others call this ‘Hume’s Law’.

Hume concluded that vice and virtue are not perceived by reason alone; moral distinctions come from sentiments of approval and disapproval. Few of his passages are more disputed, and some read the is/ought point as a narrower claim about reason.

Philippa Foot’s Natural Goodness (2001) argues that a wolf that hunts alone rather than with its pack is defective, judged by facts about its species’ way of life, and that human goodness can be judged the same way.

title: A map of ethics
description: Normative ethics offers three main approaches, consequences, duty and character, while metaethics steps back to ask what morality itself is.

facts.text: Virtue ethics is one of three major approaches in normative ethics, alongside deontology (duties or rules) and consequentialism (consequences): asked why to help someone in need, a utilitarian cites maximizing well-being, a deontologist a moral rule, a virtue ethicist charity or benevolence.

Metaethics steps back from particular moral debates to ask about morality itself: whether there are moral facts, whether moral standards are culturally relative and how we could know them; its puzzles include the Euthyphro problem and is/ought.

title: Plato’s just city
description: Plato’s Republic argues that philosophers should rule, and that a city is just when its three classes, like the soul’s three parts, each do their own work.

facts.text: In the Republic (Book VI), Socrates compares a city to a ship whose quarrelling sailors, untrained in navigation, seize the helm and mock the true pilot, who studies stars and winds, as a stargazer.
In the Republic, Socrates says cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers are kings, or kings and princes take up philosophy (473c-d).
The ideal city of Plato’s Republic has three classes: ruling guardians, auxiliary guardians who defend it, and producers who make what the city needs.
In the Republic, a city is just when each of its classes (traders, auxiliaries and guardians) does its own work and does not meddle in the others’.
The Republic divides the soul into three parts, reason, spirit and appetite; a person is just when all three function as they should, with reason ruling.
Plato’s philosopher-rulers are educated to know the Forms; the most important thing they study is the Form of the Good.
Socrates says the philosophers must be compelled to rule, and that the city whose rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed.

Karl Popper (1945) charged that the Republic is totalitarian: its rulers aim at the unity of the city as a whole regardless of citizens’ own interests; defenders reply that its rulers’ task is to benefit the ruled.

title: Virtue or law in ancient China
description: Confucians held that rulers should lead by virtuous example and ritual, while Legalists such as Han Fei held that impersonal laws, rewards and punishments must govern selfish people under ordinary rulers.

facts.text: Analects 2.3: guide people with edicts and punishments and they will stay out of trouble but have no sense of shame; guide them with virtue and ritual and they will have shame and reform themselves.
The Analects (12.19) compares the influence of the exemplary person on the people to wind blowing over grass, which bends.

The fa tradition, usually called Legalism, flourished in the Warring States period (453-221 BCE); its thinkers held that people stay selfish and must be governed by impersonal laws, rewards and punishments.
The word fa was first associated with precision tools such as T-squares, compasses, weights and measures, trusted more than an artisan’s individual skill.
Han Fei (died 233 BCE) argued that government must not rest on rulers being virtuous: exceptional rulers are rare and most are mediocre, so it must run well under ordinary ones.

title: Machiavelli’s Prince
description: Machiavelli advised rulers that it is safer to be feared than loved and to be both lion and fox, advice that made his name a byword for cunning.

facts.text: After the Medici retook Florence, Machiavelli was dismissed, then wrongly suspected of conspiracy, imprisoned and tortured in early 1513; he wrote The Prince that year, partly to regain his standing in politics, and it was published in 1532, after his death.
In The Prince, Machiavelli says a ruler should wish to be both loved and feared, but since it is difficult to unite them, it is much safer to be feared than loved.
Machiavelli’s reason: people are fickle, so love is a bond they break whenever it suits them, but fear holds them by a dread of punishment that never fails.
Machiavelli adds that a prince must be feared without being hated, which he manages above all by keeping his hands off his subjects’ property.
Machiavelli advises a prince to be both fox and lion: the lion cannot defend itself against traps and the fox cannot defend itself against wolves.
In The Prince, Machiavelli sets aside republics and principalities that ‘have never been known or seen’ to write about how people actually live, a challenge to utopian schemes such as Plato’s.
In the sixteenth century Machiavelli was denounced as an apostle of the Devil, and ‘Machiavellian’ now means marked by cunning, duplicity or bad faith.
Leo Strauss (1958) called Machiavelli a ‘teacher of evil’; Quentin Skinner (1978) read him more mildly, stressing his advice to do good if possible but evil if compelled.

title: Mill’s harm principle
description: Mill argued that power may rightfully be used over someone against their will only to prevent harm to others; Devlin replied that law may defend a society’s shared morality.

facts.text: In On Liberty (1859), Mill argued that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be used over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others, whether by legal penalties or the pressure of public opinion; over their own body and mind, individuals are sovereign.
For Mill, a person’s own good is not a sufficient warrant for compelling them: it is a good reason to reason with, persuade or entreat them, but not to force them.
Mill distinguished harm, which sets back people’s important interests, from mere offense, and harm prevention is the one justification he recognizes for restricting liberty.

Mill’s example: someone about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe may be seized and turned back if there is no time to warn them, since they do not want to fall into the river; where there is only a risk, they should only be warned.

Lord Patrick Devlin (The Enforcement of Morals, 1965) argued that a society is constituted by a shared morality that, if unenforced, lets it disintegrate, so society may defend it by law even against conduct that harms no one.
H. L. A. Hart replied that some shared morality is essential to any society, but a change in a society’s morality is not the destruction of that society.

title: Wollstonecraft’s rights of woman
description: Wollstonecraft argued in 1792 that women appeared less rational only because they were educated to please rather than to reason, against Rousseau’s Emile.

facts.text: Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792, answering Talleyrand’s plan for French schools, which would have given girls only a domestic education.
In Emile (1762), Rousseau argued that since men and women are not constituted alike they should not be educated alike, and he educated his heroine Sophie to please her husband Emile.
Wollstonecraft blamed women’s apparent weakness on ‘a false system of education’, written by men more anxious to make women alluring than rational.
Wollstonecraft wrote that, ‘taught from their infancy, that beauty is woman’s sceptre, the mind shapes itself to the body, and, roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adorn its prison.’
The Vindication wanted women educated to be rational and self-governing, taught skills to support themselves so they need not marry for money, and even given elected representatives of their own.

title: Marx on alienated work
description: Marx argued that workers under capitalism are alienated from their product, their work, others and their human nature; critics question his view of human nature and his theory of exploitation.

facts.text: In his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, unpublished at his death, Marx named four ways workers under capitalism are alienated: from their product, their work, other people and their own human nature.
On Marx’s account, workers create a product they neither own nor control, which comes to dominate them, and are forced to work in ways that are mentally or physically draining.
Marx held that work could be creative and fulfilling, a central part of what it is to be human, and rejected the view of work as a necessary evil.
Marx’s alienation charge rests on a claim about human nature: someone who held people are by nature solitary and selfish could grant that capitalist work breeds isolation yet deny it is alienation.

Robert Nozick (1974) objected that Marx’s theory of exploitation depends on the labour theory of value, that a good’s value is set by the labour in it, so if that theory fails, the exploitation charge collapses too.

title: Beauvoir and woman as the Other
description: Beauvoir argued in The Second Sex that woman has been made man’s Other and that one becomes a woman through a social role; Spelman objected that she generalized from white, middle-class lives.

facts.text: Simone de Beauvoir published The Second Sex in 1949; it found both an eager audience and harsh critics, and the Vatican placed it on its Index of prohibited books.
Beauvoir argued that man casts himself as the Subject, the Absolute, and woman as the Other, ‘the incidental, the inessential’; measured by a male standard, women are judged inferior.
Beauvoir’s line ‘One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman’ targets the view that being a woman is a biological fact; she described women as shaped into a role by social and historical conditions.
Beauvoir argued that men have been able to express their freedom through projects (transcendence), while women have been forced into repetitive, uncreative lives (immanence).
Beauvoir held that many women are partly complicit in being the Other, because the role brings benefits and relief from responsibility.
Elizabeth Spelman (Inessential Woman, 1988) argued that feminist philosophers, Beauvoir among them, ignored race, class and culture, treating white, middle-class women’s lives as all women’s.

title: Rawls’s veil of ignorance
description: Rawls asks people to choose principles of justice without knowing their place in society and argues they would choose equal liberties and the difference principle; Harsanyi argued for average utility.

facts.text: John Rawls set out his theory of justice as fairness in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice.

Rawls’s original position has people choose principles of justice behind a ‘veil of ignorance’: they know general facts about society but not their own class, talents, values or even their society’s history.

Rawls held the parties would choose equal basic liberties for all, such as freedom of thought and conscience, and allow inequalities only with fair equality of opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle).
Rawls’s maximin rule picks the option whose worst outcome is best; he says to choose as if your enemy were to assign your place in society.
The economist John Harsanyi (1975) argued that rational parties would treat every social position as equally likely and so choose the principle of average utility instead.
Rawls denied his parties are risk-averse by temperament, replying that it is rational to choose cautiously when fundamental rights and liberties are at stake.

title: Nozick’s Wilt Chamberlain
description: Nozick’s Wilt Chamberlain case argues that free exchanges from a just start produce just holdings, so liberty upsets any pattern; Cohen replied that wealth brings power over others.

facts.text: Robert Nozick (1938-2002) set out his entitlement theory of justice in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974).
In Nozick’s example, one million fans each pay 25 cents to watch Wilt Chamberlain play, leaving him with $250,000, much more than anyone else.
Nozick argued that since everyone’s starting share was just and each fan paid voluntarily, while non-fans kept their money, no one has grounds for complaint, so the new distribution is just.
Nozick’s entitlement theory: a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to their holdings, having acquired them justly or by voluntary transfer, however unequal it is.
Nozick concluded that ‘liberty upsets patterns’: keeping any pattern, including Rawls’s difference principle, would mean forbidding free exchanges or constantly undoing their results.

Critics including G. A. Cohen (‘How Patterns Preserve Liberty’, 1977) replied that Chamberlain’s wealth brings power: he can buy property and pass his fortune on, shaping others’ lives, so free exchanges can leave others less free.

title: Justice and the good society compared
description: Thinkers in this chapter disagree about who should rule, how far liberty may be limited and whether justice is a pattern of shares or a history of free exchanges.

facts.text: Plato wanted philosophers trained in knowledge to rule, while Han Fei argued that government must work under ordinary, mediocre rulers bound by impersonal laws.
Rawls’s difference principle judges a distribution by how its worst-off position fares, while Nozick’s entitlement theory judges holdings by their history, how they were acquired and transferred.

title: Determinism and the threat to free will
description: Determinism holds that the past and the laws of nature fix everything that follows, as in Laplace’s all-knowing intellect; it seems to leave no room to choose otherwise, though whether it is true is debated.
