facts.text: Determinism holds that, given the way things are at one time, the way things go thereafter is fixed as a matter of natural law.
Determinism differs from fatalism, the thesis that certain events are destined to occur no matter what we do, through gods, foreknowledge or fate rather than natural law.

In his Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814), the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intelligence knowing all forces and positions at one instant, for which “nothing would be uncertain”.
Laplace’s intelligence is often called Laplace’s demon, but Laplace himself did not use the word “demon”; it was a later embellishment.

Determinism seems to threaten free will: if the state of the world long ago fixes everything I do, and I can change neither the past nor the laws of nature, it is hard to see how I could have chosen otherwise.
Whether determinism is true is debated: many physicists have held that quantum theories are indeterministic, though philosophers of physics note that this argument is itself debatable.
Even in a deterministic world, studies of chaos suggest that no finite agent inside the world could compute its actual future, so determinism and predictability come apart.
Compatibilists argue that freedom is fully compatible with determinism.

title: Libertarian free will
description: Libertarians hold that some free choices are not fixed by prior causes and that blame needs real alternatives; agent-causal versions (Reid, Chisholm) make the agent the cause, and critics raise the luck objection.

facts.text: When we regret a foolish choice or blame ourselves for not doing what we should have done, we assume that we could have chosen and done otherwise.

Libertarians about free will hold that we have free will and that a free action must not be causally determined by factors beyond the agent’s control; most think the freedom to do otherwise is needed for moral responsibility.
If someone is coerced by a bully into stealing a lunch, blaming them no longer seems appropriate: once the alternatives are gone, blame seems unfair.
Incompatibilists argue that we act freely and are morally responsible only if we are the ultimate source of our actions, which determinism would rule out.
Agent-causal libertarians, including Thomas Reid (1788) and Roderick Chisholm, hold that in a free choice the agent herself, not just her prior mental states, causes the choice.

Roderick Chisholm wrote in 1964: “Each of us, when we act, is a prime mover unmoved. In doing what we do, we cause certain events to happen, and nothing, or no one, causes us to cause these events to happen.”
The luck objection: if nothing prior to a choice settles which way it goes, the difference between choosing one way and another seems a matter of luck, nature’s roll of the dice.
Robert Kane replies that when an agent makes an effort of will to do what she believes she ought and succeeds, indeterminism does not undermine her responsibility for the choice.

title: Compatibilism
description: Compatibilists such as Hobbes and Hume hold that freedom is doing what you will without impediment, so it fits determinism, like Hobbes’s water in its channel; van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument replies.

facts.text: Compatibilists hold that free will and determinism can both be true; the classical form was developed by Hobbes and Hume, for whom freedom is doing what you will without external impediment.
Hobbes wrote in Leviathan that a free man’s liberty consists in this: that “he finds no stop, in doing what he has the will, desire, or inclination to doe”.
In Leviathan (1651), Hobbes wrote: “Liberty and Necessity are Consistent: As in the water, that hath not only Liberty, but a Necessity of descending by the Channel.”
Hobbes held that voluntary actions proceed from the will, and so from liberty, yet every act of will has causes in a continual chain, and so proceeds from necessity.

In his Enquiry (1748), Hume called the dispute merely verbal and defined liberty as “a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will”, which belongs to everyone “who is not a prisoner and in chains”.

Peter van Inwagen’s Consequence Argument: if determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws of nature and events before we were born; neither is up to us, so our present acts are not up to us.
Many compatibilists think the Consequence Argument unsound, but it set the agenda for many contemporary compatibilist theories, which owe it a reply.

title: Frankfurt cases
description: Harry Frankfurt’s 1969 case of Black, who never has to intervene, suggests responsibility does not require the power to do otherwise; critics reply with flickers of freedom.

facts.text: The principle of alternate possibilities says a person is morally responsible for what she has done only if she could have done otherwise; it was a standard assumption of Greek, medieval and early modern thought, and combined with determinism it would mean no one is ever morally responsible.
In Harry Frankfurt’s 1969 case, Black wants Jones to perform an action and is ready to intervene if Jones is about to decide otherwise, but Jones decides on his own and Black never acts.
Frankfurt leaves Black’s method open, suggesting a terrible threat, a potion, hypnosis or manipulating Jones’s brain.
Frankfurt concluded that Jones is just as responsible as if Black had not existed, though he could not have done otherwise, so the principle of alternate possibilities is false.
If Frankfurt is right, then even if determinism removed the freedom to do otherwise, that alone would not show that people cannot be morally responsible.

Critics note that Black acts only on a prior sign of Jones’s inclination, so Jones keeps small alternatives, called “flickers of freedom”; Frankfurt’s allies reply that these are too thin to ground responsibility.

title: Sartre on freedom and bad faith
description: Sartre held that for humans existence precedes essence, so we are condemned to be free, and that denying this is bad faith, like his café waiter; Merleau-Ponty stressed freedom within a situation.

facts.text: Many thousands of Parisians packed into Sartre’s public lecture Existentialism is a Humanism towards the end of 1945; it gave an accessible version of Being and Nothingness (1943).
Sartre’s example: a paper-knife is made by an artisan who had a conception of what it is and what it is for, so for manufactured things essence precedes existence.
Sartre held that for humans “existence precedes essence”: a person first exists, turns up in the world, and only afterwards defines himself; no pre-given nature determines us.
Sartre said man is “condemned to be free”: condemned because he did not create himself, yet free, and responsible for everything he does.

Sartre’s best-known example of bad faith, in Being and Nothingness, is a café waiter whose movements are a little too precise, who plays at being a waiter as if his role fixed what he does, while at some level aware he is deceiving himself.
Maurice Merleau-Ponty held that our options are embedded in a social and historical situation “before any personal decision has been made”: “We choose the world, and the world chooses us.”
Sartre himself later called the idea of radical, unconditioned freedom “nonsense”, saying freedom must be understood as freedom-in-situation.

title: Locke’s memory theory of personal identity
description: Locke held that a person is the same as far as consciousness reaches back, so a prince’s consciousness in a cobbler’s body is still the prince; Reid’s brave officer and Butler’s circularity objection reply.

facts.text: John Locke added his chapter on persons and personal identity (Book 2, Chapter 27) to the second edition of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding in 1694.
Locke defined a person as a thinking intelligent being that can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places, and called “person” a forensic term.
Locke imagined the soul of a prince, with all his princely thoughts, entering the body of a cobbler; the person would then be the prince, because a person goes where their consciousness goes.
For Locke, personal identity reaches as far back as consciousness extends to past actions and thoughts, and the same person is distinct from the same man, the human body.
Thomas Reid (1785) objected with a brave officer flogged as a boy, who remembers it when he takes an enemy standard, but as an old general remembers the standard and not the flogging.
On Locke’s view, Reid argued, the general is the same person as the boy by the chain of memories, yet is not, because he cannot remember the flogging.
Joseph Butler (1736) objected that consciousness of personal identity presupposes, and therefore cannot constitute, personal identity.

title: The Ship of Theseus
description: Plutarch’s ship, repaired plank by plank, and Hobbes’s second ship rebuilt from the old planks ask what makes a thing the same over time; constitution theorists and Chisholm answer differently.

facts.text: Plutarch reports that the Athenians kept the thirty-oared ship in which Theseus returned from Crete to the time of Demetrius Phalereus, replacing decayed planks with new timber, and philosophers argued over whether it stayed the same ship.

The 17th-century philosopher Thomas Hobbes imagined someone keeping the old planks and putting them together again in the same order, leaving two ships with a claim to be the original, which he called absurd.
In the puzzle, the repaired ship is indistinguishable from the original but has entirely different planks, while the reassembled ship has all and only the original planks.
Constitution theorists answer that the repaired ship is the original ship, while the reassembled ship is only made of the same planks and is not identical with it.
Roderick Chisholm held that an object cannot survive losing any of its parts, so the repaired ship counts as the same only in a loose and popular sense.

title: Parfit’s teleporter and fission
description: Derek Parfit’s teletransporter and fission cases led him to conclude that psychological continuity, not identity, is what matters in survival; critics argue identity still matters.

facts.text: Derek Parfit, in Reasons and Persons (1984), imagined a teletransporter that records an exact blueprint of you, destroys the original and sends the information to Mars, where a duplicate is built from new matter.
The duplicate on Mars shares all your memories, character traits and other psychological features, which raises the question whether it is you.
In fission cases, each half of a brain is transplanted into a different body, and both resulting people are psychologically continuous with the original, though they are not each other.
Parfit concluded that in fission the original person, strictly, survives as neither result, yet having two such survivors is about as good as ordinary survival.
Parfit argued that what matters in survival is psychological continuity, not personal identity itself.
On Parfit’s reductionism, a person’s existence consists in nothing over and above the existence of a brain and body and an interrelated series of mental and physical events.
Critics such as Ernest Sosa and Trenton Merricks argue that identity does matter: that a future person is me gives me a special reason to care about him.
Kathleen Wilkes doubted that fission cases, which assume a division of the lower brain that is not physically possible, can settle questions of personal identity.

title: Ubuntu and the relational self
description: Ubuntu, from southern African Nguni languages, holds that a person is a person through other persons; Menkiti says personhood is attained through communal life, and Eze warns against submerging the individual.

facts.text: The Zulu and Ndebele maxim umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu translates as “a person is a person through other persons”.
Ubuntu is a word in southern African Bantu languages including Zulu, Xhosa and Ndebele, all Nguni languages, for the moral quality of being a person; Mogobe Ramose defined it as humaneness.
Thaddeus Metz reads the maxim as saying that one’s identity as a human being causally and even metaphysically depends on a community.
The Nigerian philosopher Ifeanyi Menkiti wrote in 1984 that personhood has to be attained, in proportion as one takes part in communal life and carries out one’s obligations.
In Akan, a person whose conduct is persistently cruel or selfish may be said to be “not a person” (onnye onipa), while still being acknowledged as a human being.

Desmond Tutu, who chaired South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, helped make ubuntu widely known; in No Future Without Forgiveness (1999) he called ubuntu “the single main ingredient” behind its achievements.

Michael Onyebuchi Eze criticizes writers who glorify community over the individual and romanticize the past, arguing that individual and community are “not radically opposed” but form each other together.

title: Freedom and the self compared
description: The free will debate (determinism, libertarianism, compatibilism, Frankfurt, Sartre) and the personal identity debate (Locke, the ship, Parfit, ubuntu) meet at who is responsible for what.

facts.text: The free will and personal identity debates meet at moral responsibility: who can be held accountable for an act, and whether they could have done otherwise.

title: Plato’s cave as an argument
description: Plato’s cave argues that the senses show only shadows of reality, known fully by thought, and that education turns the soul around; Aristotle and the empiricists rejected its two worlds.

facts.text: In Book VII of Plato’s Republic, Socrates pictures prisoners chained since childhood in an underground den, able to look only ahead at shadows cast by a fire behind them; to them the truth would be nothing but the shadows, and they are ’like ourselves’.

A freed prisoner is pained by the light and thinks the shadows truer; dragged up, he sees shadows, then reflections in water, then things, then the sun; back in the den he looks ridiculous, and the prisoners would kill anyone who tried to lead them up.
Socrates says the prison is the world of sight and the climb is the soul’s ascent into the intellectual world, where the Form of the Good is seen last of all.

Socrates concludes that education is not putting knowledge into the soul ’like sight into blind eyes’: the power to learn is already there, and the whole soul must be turned from the world of becoming toward being.

Empiricists reject the thesis, which Plato’s view of eternal Forms beyond sense experience supports, that we have knowledge built in independent of experience; John Locke devoted the whole first book of his Essay to attacking it.

title: Zeno’s Achilles and the tortoise
description: Zeno argued Achilles can never catch a tortoise because he faces infinitely many catch-ups; the usual reply is that an infinite series can have a finite sum, though some question whether infinitely many tasks can be completed.

facts.text: Zeno of Elea (born about 490 BCE) wrote a now-lost book of paradoxes defending Parmenides, his mentor, who held that reality is one and unchanging and that change is an illusion; his arguments survive mainly through Aristotle.
Zeno’s paradoxes suppose his opponents’ views true for argument’s sake and show that absurd conclusions follow from them.
In the Achilles, the tortoise has a head start; each time Achilles reaches where it was, it has moved on, so he has infinitely many catch-ups to make, and Zeno concludes he never catches it.

The standard reply is that an infinite series can have a finite sum: eat half a cake, then half the rest, forever, and you eat exactly one cake; so infinitely many catch-ups fit a finite distance and time. A rigorous theory of such sums came from Cauchy in the 19th century.

Bertrand Russell held that Achilles completes infinitely many tasks in a finite time; in 1954 James Thomson described a lamp switched on for half a minute, off for a quarter, on for an eighth and so on, arguing such a supertask is impossible since the lamp can be neither on nor off after it.

title: Augustine’s puzzle of time
description: Augustine found that past, future and a lengthless present all seem not to exist, and located time in the mind as memory, attention and expectation; Aristotle instead tied time to change.

facts.text: In Book 11 of the Confessions (E. B. Pusey’s translation), Augustine writes: ’What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.’

Augustine argues that the past is no longer and the future not yet, while any stretch of the present splits into past and future parts, so ’the present hath no space’; a present that never passed into the past would be eternity, not time.
Augustine says there are three times in the soul: a present of things past (memory), a present of things present (sight, or attention) and a present of things future (expectation).

Reciting a psalm he knows, Augustine notes, his expectation first covers the whole, then shrinks as memory grows, until all has passed into memory; he calls time a distention, or stretching, of the soul itself.
Aristotle held that there is no time without change and that time is the measure of change: a change can be faster or slower, but time itself cannot.

Aristotle asked whether there would be time without a soul to count it and answered that if only a soul can count, there could be change but no time; Augustine’s account in Confessions 11, which locates time in the mind’s memory, attention and expectation, is often called subjectivist.

title: Why is there something rather than nothing?
description: Leibniz’s principle of sufficient reason leads him to ask why anything exists and to answer with a necessary being; critics such as Russell reply that the universe may be a brute fact.

facts.text: Leibniz (1646-1716) was the first to call the principle of sufficient reason by name and treat it as a major principle of philosophy; in Principles of Nature and Grace (1714) he states that nothing comes about without a sufficient reason why it is so rather than otherwise.
Leibniz writes that, given this principle, the first question we can fairly ask is why there is something rather than nothing, since ’nothing is simpler and easier than something’.

Leibniz argues that the sufficient reason for the universe cannot lie in the series of contingent things, where each motion comes from an earlier one and the question ’Why?’ remains, but must lie outside it in a necessary being carrying the reason for its existence within itself, ’what we call God’.
In his 1948 radio debate with Frederick Copleston, Bertrand Russell denied that the universe needs an explanation: it is ’just there, and that’s all’.

In Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Cleanthes argues that once the causes of each of twenty particles of matter are shown, asking for the cause of the whole twenty is unreasonable: the whole is explained in explaining the parts.

title: The ontological argument
description: Anselm argued from the idea of that than which nothing greater can be conceived to its existence; Gaunilo replied with a perfect island and Kant with the claim that existence is not a real predicate.

facts.text: In his Proslogion (1078), Anselm argues from a priori premises: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; even the fool understands this, and if it existed only in the understanding, a greater one, existing in reality too, could be conceived, so it exists.

Gaunilo of Marmoutiers, a monk and contemporary of Anselm, replied in On Behalf of the Fool that the same reasoning would prove that an island more excellent than all other lands exists, showing the argument’s form is flawed.

Anselm replied that his argument applies only to that than which nothing greater can be conceived; defenders add that an island has no intrinsic maximum (more fruit can always be imagined), so ’the greatest possible island’ is incoherent.

In the Critique of Pure Reason, Kant writes that ’Being is evidently not a real predicate’: saying a thing exists adds nothing to its concept, so a hundred real thalers (Meiklejohn translates ’dollars’) contain no more than a hundred possible ones, though the real ones add to one’s wealth.

title: The cosmological argument
description: Al-Ghazali and Aquinas argued from chains of causes to a first cause; Russell asked what caused the first cause, and defenders reply that their premises do not say everything has a cause.

facts.text: Al-Ghazali (died 1111) argued that everything that begins to exist requires a cause of its beginning; since a series of past events cannot go back to infinity, the world had a beginning and so has a cause.

In Aquinas’s Second Way (Summa Theologica I, q.2, a.3), nothing is the efficient cause of itself, and efficient causes cannot go on to infinity, since taking away the first cause takes away the rest; so there is a first efficient cause, ’to which everyone gives the name of God’.
Aquinas held that the world could in principle have always existed; his argument is for a first cause on which everything depends, not a first cause in time, unlike the kalam version.

In Why I Am Not a Christian (1927), Russell says a line read at 18 in Mill’s Autobiography (’Who made me?’ suggests ’Who made God?’) showed the fallacy: ’If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause’; if anything can be uncaused, it may as well be the world.
Defenders reply that no major version rests on the premise that everything has a cause: the kalam premise covers only what begins to exist, and Aquinas argues for a first, non-dependent cause.

title: The design argument
description: Paley inferred a designer from a watch and the eye; Hume questioned the analogy, Darwin offered natural selection, and fine-tuning arguments and their critics carry the debate to physics.

facts.text: In Natural Theology (1802), William Paley contrasts a stone on a heath, which might have lain there forever, with a watch, whose parts are framed and put together for a purpose, so it must have had a maker.
Paley applies the same inference to nature, arguing there is ’precisely the same proof that the eye was made for vision as there is that the telescope was made for assisting it’.

In Hume’s Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Philo says ’the world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch’, and that for all we know it was ’the first rude essay of some infant deity’.

Darwin’s natural selection explains adaptation by undesigned, chance variations that are kept or eliminated as organisms survive, producing organisms well fitted to their niches with no intention behind them.

Darwin, who as a student was delighted by the logic of Paley’s Natural Theology, later wrote that ’the old argument from design in Nature, as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered’.

Fine-tuning arguments note that life would be impossible if about two dozen properties of the universe were even slightly different; George Schlesinger argued design best explains this, while critics reply that other forms of life might be possible or that ours may be one universe in a multiverse.
Darwinian theories explain how complex organisms developed from simpler ones and do not purport to explain the origin of the first life.

title: The problem of evil
description: The problem of evil asks how an all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good God is consistent with evil; Augustine and Plantinga reply with free will, and critics answer with natural evil.

facts.text: The problem of evil is traditionally attributed to Epicurus, though the attribution is uncertain; in Hume’s Dialogues, Philo states ’Epicurus’s old questions’: is God willing but not able, able but not willing, or both able and willing, and if so, ’whence then is evil?’
In 1955 J. L. Mackie argued that ’God is omnipotent’, ’God is omniscient’, ’God is perfectly good’ and ’evil exists’ cannot all be true, calling religious beliefs ’positively irrational’.
Augustine held that free will is a great good, but not an absolute one, and is liable to misuse, and so is the source of moral evil.

Alvin Plantinga’s free will defense (1974) holds that a world of significantly free creatures doing more good than evil is more valuable, and that God cannot cause creatures to do only what is right freely; as a ’defense’ it aims only to show consistency, not God’s actual reasons.
Critics object that natural evils such as disease, famine and earthquakes result from no one’s choice, so free will does not explain them.

Mackie argued that an omnipotent God could have made beings who act freely but always go right; Plantinga agrees such a world is possible but says whether it is actual depends on what free creatures would do, not on God alone.

title: Wittgenstein: meaning as use
description: The later Wittgenstein held that a word’s meaning is, in many cases, its use, that words like ’game’ are linked by family resemblance, and that some philosophical puzzles come from language misleading us.

facts.text: Wittgenstein’s Philosophical Investigations, published after his death in 1953, says (section 43) that for a large class of cases ’the meaning of a word is its use in the language’, rather than an object it names or a feeling.

In section 11 he writes: ’Think of the tools in a tool-box: there is a hammer, pliers, a saw, a screw-driver’, a rule, a glue-pot; the functions of words are as diverse as the functions of these objects.

Looking at games, Wittgenstein finds no one feature common to all, only ’a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing’, which he calls family resemblance, rejecting the search for one essential core such as a Platonic form.

Wittgenstein held that philosophical confusions arise from misleading analogies between forms of expression, such as ’I’ll keep it in mind’ and ’I’ll keep it in this box’, which make the mind seem a mysterious box; the remedy is to recall how such words are actually used.
Wittgenstein wrote that the aim of philosophy is ’to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle’ (section 309).

In My Philosophical Development (1959), Bertrand Russell, Wittgenstein’s former teacher, wrote that he had not found in the Philosophical Investigations ’anything that seemed to me interesting’ and did not understand why a whole school found important wisdom in its pages.
Wittgenstein is one of the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, regarded by some as the most important since Kant.

title: Reality, time and God compared
description: The chapter’s arguments start either from reason alone or from the observed world, and their critics often answer with the other tool.

facts.text: Ontological arguments proceed from a priori premises alone, while cosmological and design arguments start from features of the world we observe, such as chains of causes and parts suited to a purpose.

title: The trolley problem
description: Philippa Foot’s 1967 runaway tram, paired with a judge who could frame an innocent man, asks whether diverting harm onto one to save five is allowed, and why the numbers alone don’t settle it.

facts.text: In 1967 Philippa Foot imagined the driver of a runaway tram who can only steer it from one track to another, with five people on one track and one person on the other; she held it is not wrong for him to steer toward the one.
Foot paired the tram with a judge who could stop rioters from killing five people only by framing one innocent man; she held the judge must not, though the driver may steer toward the one.

Foot explained the difference by doing and allowing, holding that not harming weighs more than helping: the judge chooses between killing one and allowing five to die, while the driver chooses between killing one and killing five.
Judith Jarvis Thomson changed Foot’s driver into a bystander at a switch, who would kill one rather than let five die; turning still seemed permissible to many, which undermined Foot’s explanation.
In 2008 Thomson argued against the consensus that the bystander may turn the trolley: since few would turn it onto themselves, they may not turn it onto a stranger, like stealing to give to charity.

title: The footbridge and double effect
description: Judith Jarvis Thomson’s footbridge case keeps five for one but makes the harm a means; the doctrine of double effect explains the difference by separating intended means from foreseen side effects, and critics raise the problem of closeness.

facts.text: Judith Jarvis Thomson’s 1985 footbridge case, based on Foot’s 1967 examples: the only way to stop a trolley heading for five people who cannot escape is to push a stranger off a bridge onto the track.
Many people believe it would be wrong to push a bystander onto the track to stop the trolley, yet permissible to switch it onto a track with one person.
Thomas Aquinas is credited with introducing the principle of double effect, which separates grave harm caused as a means to a good end from grave harm caused only as a foreseen side effect.
On double effect, the death at the switch is a foreseen side effect of diverting the trolley, while pushing a person in front of it makes their death part of the plan for saving the five.
Critics raise the problem of closeness: it is hard to tell harms foreseen as side effects from harms so close to the means that they must be intended, and no clear resolution has emerged.

Philosophers split over double effect and the trolley: some take the paired intuitions as proof of it, Thomson (2008) denied switching is allowed, and McIntyre denied double effect explains switching.

title: Singer’s drowning child
description: Peter Singer’s 1972 shallow-pond case supports a principle that we ought to prevent very bad things when we can do so without sacrificing anything morally significant; critics press the demandingness objection.

facts.text: In “Famine, Affluence, and Morality” (1972), Peter Singer wrote that walking past a shallow pond with a child drowning in it, he ought to wade in, though his clothes get muddy.
Singer held that muddy clothes are insignificant while the child’s death would be very bad; letting the child drown strikes most people as monstrous.

Singer’s argument runs on premises: if it is in our power to prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything morally significant, we ought to; suffering and death from lack of food, shelter or medical care are very bad; giving can prevent some of it.
Singer concluded we are all like the person passing the pond: the cost of a new shirt or a night out can mean the difference between life and death for someone elsewhere.
Singer argued that distance makes no moral difference: a person in need far away counts as much as one nearby, because what matters is your ability to help at low cost.

A common criticism of Singer’s argument is the demandingness objection: commonsense morality treats charity as good but optional, and the world’s needs never stop, so helping would take over your life.
Singer’s defenders reply that his moderate principle asks you to give up only what is not morally significant, which leaves room for the personal projects that matter most to you.

title: Animals and suffering
description: Bentham and Singer make the capacity to suffer the test of whose interests count, with equal consideration of like interests; Aristotle and Kant ranked animals below humans, and Kant allowed only indirect duties regarding them.

facts.text: Jeremy Bentham wrote (1789) that the question is not “Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?”: the capacity to suffer marks whose interests count.
Peter Singer’s principle of equal consideration of interests gives equal weight in moral deliberation to the like interests of all those affected by our actions, animals included.
Richard Ryder coined “speciesism” in the 1970s for a human-centred prejudice he compared to racism; Peter Singer popularized the term.
Aristotle held a natural hierarchy of living beings: humans can use reason to guide conduct while animals rely on instinct, so the function of animals is to serve the needs of human beings.
Kant held we have only indirect duties regarding animals, owed to humanity, yet condemned cruelty because “he who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men.”
Critics call the indirect view unsatisfying: it makes cruelty to an animal wrong because of its effect on the person, failing to capture the wrong done to the animal itself.
Indirect theorists reply that even without direct moral status for animals, we may have demanding duties regarding how we treat them, such as a duty not to be cruel.

title: The murderer at the door
description: Kant’s 1797 reply to Benjamin Constant holds that truthfulness is an unconditional duty even toward a murderer asking where your friend is; consequentialists reply that lying to save a life is permitted.

facts.text: Benjamin Constant (1797) wrote that a duty to tell the truth, taken unconditionally, would make society impossible; truth is owed only to someone with a right to it, and no one has a right to a truth that injures others.
Constant’s example: a German philosopher held that lying to a murderer who asks whether your friend, whom he is pursuing, has taken refuge in your house would be a crime.

Kant replied in a 1797 essay that truthfulness in statements one cannot avoid is a duty to everyone, however great the disadvantage, and that to be truthful is “a sacred unconditional command of reason”.

Kant argued a lie always injures another, if not an individual then humanity, because it makes declarations in general find no credit; truthfulness is the basis of duties founded on contract, which even the least exception would make uncertain.

Kant argued that if you lie that your friend is not home, but he has slipped out unseen and meets the murderer, you could justly be accused as the cause; whoever lies must answer for the consequences.

Consequentialism holds that whether an act is right depends only on its consequences; consequentialists and moderate deontologists, from Constant to Mill and Sidgwick, hold lying to a would-be murderer permissible.

title: Moral luck
description: Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel showed that our judgments of blame depend on luck, such as how things turn out for two equally careless drivers, clashing with the principle that we are assessable only for what we control.

facts.text: Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel published a now classic pair of papers, both called “Moral Luck”, in 1976; Williams expected the phrase to suggest an oxymoron.
Kant wrote that a good will, even if it achieved nothing, would still shine like a jewel by itself, as something with its full worth in itself; Nagel cites the passage.
The Control Principle: we are morally assessable only for what depends on factors under our control; so two people differing only in factors beyond their control should not be judged differently.
If a woman who stepped on your toes was simply pushed, the temptation to blame her evaporates, which supports the Control Principle.

Two otherwise conscientious drivers both forgot to have their brakes checked and both have brake failure, but only one finds a child in the path of the car; judging them differently is resultant moral luck.
Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck, now called resultant (luck in how things turn out), circumstantial, constitutive and causal.
Adam Smith held that all praise and blame ultimately belong to the intention of the heart; many philosophers deny moral luck, saying luck changes only how clearly we can see someone’s fault.
Nagel replied that luck affects our intentions and willings too, through circumstance and character, so retreating to intentions does not escape it.

title: Impartial care or family first
description: Mozi’s inclusive care (jian ai) asks people to be concerned for everyone as for their own; Mencius and the Confucians defended care with distinctions that begins in the family and extends outward.

facts.text: The Mohists’ best-known teaching is jian ai, usually rendered “inclusive care” or “impartial concern”: being concerned for the welfare of others without distinguishing self and others, associates and strangers.

The Mohists argued that crime, strife and war come from caring for one’s own family, city or state and not others’, asking who would attack another state if people were for others’ states as for their own.
In a Mohist thought experiment, you are leaving on a long journey and must entrust your family to someone; the Mohists claimed even partial people would choose an impartial carer.
Chad Hansen and Bryan Van Norden object that the journey case shows only that partial people want others to be impartial, not that they have reason to act impartially themselves.

Confucians held a doctrine of care with distinctions: the Analects (1.2) calls filial piety the root of goodness, and Mencius taught that benevolence grows by extending love first shown in the family.

Mencius asked the Mohist Yi Zhi whether he truly held that affection for one’s own nephew is like affection for a neighbor’s baby: humans naturally care more for relatives, so impartiality is impractical.
Mencius equated inclusive care with renouncing one’s father and dismissed Mozi as a “beast”; many later Confucians held that inclusive care runs counter to human nature.
The Mohists replied that impartial concern is no harder than things rulers had demanded and got from subjects, such as eating less and wearing coarse clothing.

title: Duties to future people
description: Derek Parfit’s non-identity problem: because a different choice would bring different people into existence, a harmful long-term policy like depletion seems to make no one worse off, though it still seems wrong.

facts.text: Had your parents delayed conceiving a child by a few months, the odds are that a different person would exist instead of you; Gregory Kavka called this the precariousness of existence.
Derek Parfit set out the non-identity problem in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons.
In Parfit’s depletion case, a community depletes rather than conserves resources; life is slightly better for two centuries, then much lower, yet the choice changes who is conceived.

Parfit summed up the person-affecting intuition as “what is bad must be bad for someone”; with depletion it implies the choice harms no one, yet Parfit held the great lowering of quality of life gives moral reason against it.
Replies to the non-identity problem include biting the bullet that such choices are not wrong (David Boonin) and judging outcomes impersonally, as total utilitarianism does.
The non-identity problem remains among the most challenging problems in population ethics.

title: Machine moral status
description: Whether an artificial system could ever be a moral patient has no agreed answer in 2026; sentience views, Kantian rational-agency views and relational views point to different evidence.

facts.text: A moral agent has obligations; a moral patient is something moral agents have obligations towards. Humans are the typical agents and sentient animals the typical patients.
The standard view has been that AI systems have no moral status of any kind, but that view has come under pressure; as of 2026 there is no agreed answer.
In the moral status literature there is a trend toward seeing sentience as at least a necessary condition for moral status, which raises worries about creating conscious AI.
Thomas Metzinger has called for a moratorium on synthetic phenomenology, research that risks creating artificial conscious experience and so artificial suffering.
Mark Coeckelbergh and David Gunkel propose a relational turn: if we relate to robots as though they had rights, it may be futile to search for whether they really do.
Joanna Bryson has insisted that robots should not be given rights.
Kant made autonomy, the rational will to stand back from desires and choose, the property a being needs for its interests to count directly in moral assessment.

title: Reasoning through a new dilemma
description: Testing a new case such as Foot and Thomson’s Transplant against outcome counting, revised consequentialism, the doing/allowing distinction and double effect shows where the theories agree on a verdict and split on the reason.

facts.text: In the Transplant case, discussed by Foot and Thomson, five patients will die without transplants of different organs; a healthy visitor matches all five, and taking his organs would save them but end his life.
Classical utilitarianism seems to imply the surgeon should operate, since five lives outweigh one; most people find that result abominable, a violation of the donor’s rights.
Some consequentialists bite the bullet, saying such unrealistic cases shouldn’t be trusted to our intuitions; most instead revise the theory, for example by counting a killing as worse than a death.

title: Hume and Kant on beauty
description: Hume held that beauty belongs to feeling but that the joint verdict of true critics sets a standard of taste; Kant held that a judgment of beauty, though based on feeling, speaks for everyone.

facts.text: In “Of the Standard of Taste” (1757), David Hume held that beauty and deformity are not qualities in objects but belong entirely to sentiment (feeling).
Hume wrote that anyone asserting Ogilby equal in genius to Milton defends an extravagance like calling a molehill as high as a mountain (Teneriffe), and such taste is judged absurd.
In Hume’s story, two of Sancho’s kinsmen taste a hogshead of wine; one detects leather, the other iron, and both are mocked until an old key on a leather thong is found at the bottom.
Hume said true critics need strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison and freedom from prejudice, and took their joint verdict as the standard of taste.
Critics object that Hume’s standard is circular: great art is what true critics approve, but true critics are identified by approving great art.
In his Critique of Judgment (1790), Kant said that someone who calls Canary wine pleasant should say it is pleasant “to me”, since everyone has his own taste in the pleasant.
Kant held that whoever calls something beautiful “judges not merely for himself, but for every one”, speaking with a universal voice, though no rule or proof can force agreement.
Kant held that pleasure in beauty is disinterested: it is neither based on desire nor produces one.
Nietzsche attacked Kant’s separation of pleasure in beauty from desire, calling pleasure cut off from our passionate lives unrealistic and undesirable.

title: What makes something art
description: Three answers to what art is: imitation (Plato), expression of felt emotion (Tolstoy) and the institutional theory (Dickie), each with a standard objection.

facts.text: Marcel Duchamp presented an ordinary urinal as an artwork, Fountain, and said it was chosen for its lack of aesthetic features.
Plato held that the arts are mimetic (imitative): a painting copies physical things, which themselves copy the Forms, so art gives only an appearance of an appearance.
Music has always been hard for the imitation theory to explain, since instrumental music does not seem to imitate or represent anything.
Leo Tolstoy defined art as one person consciously handing on to others feelings he has lived through, so that they are infected by those feelings and experience them too.
Critics of expression theories note that a cheerful piece of music need not come from a cheerful composer: a sad composer could have written it just as well.
George Dickie’s institutional theory (1974): a work of art is an artifact on which someone acting for the artworld has conferred the status of candidate for appreciation.
Critics call the institutional theory viciously circular: artworks, artists and the artworld are each defined in terms of the others.

title: Epicurus on fearing death
description: Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us because good and bad require sensation; Lucretius added the symmetry argument; Nagel replied that death deprives us of life’s goods.

facts.text: In his Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus argued that good and evil imply sensation and death is the privation of all sensation, so death is nothing to us.
Epicurus wrote that death is nothing to us, “seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not” (Hicks translation).
Lucretius, a follower of Epicurus, argued that the endless time before our birth is like a mirror Nature holds up of the time after death, and it holds nothing to fear.

In “Death” (1970), Thomas Nagel argued that death can be bad for us because it deprives us of the goods life would have held, as missing a joyous occasion while unconscious is bad without causing pain.

title: The Stoic split
description: Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius taught that only our own judgments, aims and desires are up to us, and that we are disturbed by our views of things; Aristotle held that great misfortune can spoil a happy life.

facts.text: Epictetus spent part of his life as a slave in Rome, was freed, and later taught philosophy at his own school in Nicopolis in Greece.

The Enchiridion opens: within our power are opinion, aim, desire and aversion; beyond it are body, property, reputation and office. Treating the second as ours brings hindrance, lament and disturbance.
Epictetus wrote that “men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things” (Enchiridion 5, Higginson translation).
Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE, wrote his Meditations as private notes to himself.
Marcus Aurelius wrote: “Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged” (Meditations IV.7, Casaubon translation).
Epictetus compared us to ball players who know the ball has no value in itself yet chase it hard, because playing the game well matters: externals must be used with care but with composure.
Stoics such as Marcus Aurelius held that happiness lies in virtue, which is wholly in one’s own power.
Aristotle held that happiness needs a complete life, and that no one calls happy a man who, like Priam, meets great misfortunes in old age and dies wretched.

title: The experience machine
description: Nozick’s experience machine suggests that something besides pleasant experience matters for a life going well; De Brigard’s reversed case suggests status quo bias shapes the answer.

facts.text: Hedonism about well-being holds that pleasure is the only thing good for you in itself, and pain the only thing bad in itself.
In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Robert Nozick imagined a machine giving you any experiences you wanted, such as writing a great novel, while you could not tell they were not real.

Nozick argued we want to do certain things, not just have the experience of doing them; to be a certain sort of person, not an indeterminate blob in a tank; and to make a real difference, so something matters besides experience.
Felipe De Brigard (2010) reversed the case: told they are already in an experience machine, many people choose to stay, which he attributed to status quo bias rather than a love of reality.

title: Nietzsche’s eternal return
description: After diagnosing that “God is dead”, Nietzsche imagined a demon offering eternal recurrence as a test of whether you can affirm your life as it is; readers dispute whether it is a thought experiment or a claim about time.

facts.text: In The Gay Science (1882), Nietzsche’s madman announces that “God is dead”; Nietzsche meant that belief in the Christian God had become unbelievable, so everything built on it, including European morality, would collapse.
Nietzsche’s madman brings the news that God is dead to a crowd who already do not believe, so the point is not simply that atheism is true.

In The Gay Science (341), a demon tells you that you must live this life again innumerable times, with nothing new, “this spider and this moonlight among the trees” included; the question would lie on your actions as “the heaviest burden”.
Nietzsche asks whether you would gnash your teeth and curse the demon, or answer: “Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!”
An influential reading treats the eternal recurrence as a thought experiment testing whether your life has been good, like being asked whether you would marry your spouse again.
On one reading, imagining your finite life recurring forever blocks treating it as a test to be redeemed by a later reward, so the yes must be to this life as it is.
Nietzsche called loving what is necessary in things amor fati, love of fate, and wished someday to be only a Yes-sayer (Gay Science 276).

Early readers took the eternal recurrence as a cosmological claim that all events repeat in cycles, and critics raised problems for it on that reading; some scholars, such as Paul Loeb, still defend it.

title: Camus and the absurd
description: For Camus the absurd is the clash between our demand for meaning and the world’s silence; he answered it with lucid revolt and pictured Sisyphus happy; Nagel preferred irony.

facts.text: Camus opened The Myth of Sisyphus by saying that deciding whether or not life is worth living answers the fundamental question of philosophy.
For Camus the absurd is neither in us nor in the world but the clash between our “wild longing for clarity” and the “unreasonable silence of the world”.
Camus rejected escapes, whether hope for another life or giving up on this one, and urged living on in revolt: lucid, without consolation, aware of life’s limits.
Sisyphus pushes his rock up the mountain, watches it roll down and begins again, endlessly; Camus made him, fully conscious of his hopeless labor yet pushing on, the hero of the absurd.
The Myth of Sisyphus ends: “The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”

In “The Absurd” (1971), Thomas Nagel traced absurdity to our ability to step back and see all we take seriously as arbitrary; defiance like Camus’s might be nobler but no less absurd, and he recommended irony.

title: What makes a life meaningful
description: Three views of meaning in life: God’s purpose (supernaturalism), what you care about (subjectivism) and Susan Wolf’s hybrid of caring and real worth, each with its objection.

facts.text: Supernaturalist theories hold that a spiritual realm is central to meaning in life; some, such as William Lane Craig, argue that only God’s purpose could ground the objective values meaning needs.
Kurt Baier objected that if God had created us for a purpose, that would degrade us, since we would be expected to serve the aims of a superior being.
Subjectivists hold that meaning varies with each person’s attitudes; Harry Frankfurt argued that a life is meaningful to the extent that you care about or love something.
Critics of subjectivism, including Susan Wolf, point to lives devoted to pointless projects, such as collecting a big ball of string, that seem meaningless however much they are loved.

Susan Wolf’s hybrid view: “Meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness”; no meaning accrues from loving a worthless project or from a worthwhile one you do not care about.
Whether objective value exists, and where it comes from, is itself debated, which bears on theories like Wolf’s that require it.

title: Living forever, through the toolkit
description: Taking a new question through the philosopher’s toolkit: clarify what living forever means, test it with Williams’s Makropulos case, and weigh his tedium argument against Fischer’s and Nagel’s replies.

facts.text: Philosophers debating immortality specify which kind they mean; a common version is a life extended indefinitely without aging, staying healthy and mentally sharp.
Bernard Williams set two conditions for wanting an endless life: it should clearly be you who lives forever, and that life should relate to the aims you have now.
In “The Makropulos Case” (1973), Bernard Williams used Elina Makropulos, from a play by Karel Čapek, who took an elixir of life and at 342 has reached a state of boredom and indifference.
Williams argued that, given enough time, we would lose the deep desires that make us want a future, and oppressive boredom would set in.

Nagel, Jonathan Glover and John Martin Fischer argued that an endless life need not become dull, since interests could keep changing; Williams replied that a new set of desires and character makes it unclear the later person is you.
Williams’s claim that immortality cannot be made desirable remains controversial.
